cards.q: Why does the Malaysian STI guideline say a sexual history is important? (5 purposes)
cards.a:
• Guides the **examination and investigations** (which sites to sample)
• Ascertains **contraception use and pregnancy risk**
• Assesses other sexual health issues, incl. **psychosexual problems**
• Assesses **HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis risk** for testing and prevention
• Identifies risk behaviours to drive **health promotion and partner notification**
cards.m: History decides the swabs: no anal-sex history = no rectal swab = missed rectal gonorrhoea.

cards.q: What are the 6 Ps of a sexual history?
cards.a:
• **Partners** – gender and number in the last 3 months
• **Practices** – last sexual intercourse (LSI): when, with whom, oral/vaginal/anal, insertive or receptive
• **Protection** – condom use, last unprotected sex
• **Past history** – previous STIs in self and partners
• **Pregnancy planning**
• **Plus** – Pleasure, Problems and Pride (sexual function, gender identity support)
cards.m: Partners, Practices, Protection, Past, Pregnancy, Plus.

cards.q: Over what period are sexual partners counted in the sexual history, and what detail is needed if there are many?
cards.a:
• Count partners in the **last 3 months**
• Ask gender of partner(s)
• If **more than 5 partners**, specific details of each are not necessary
• Previous sexual intercourse (PSI) with a different partner in the last 3 months – ask the same details as for LSI

cards.q: List the general principles of conducting a sexual history consultation.
cards.a:
• Ensure **privacy and confidentiality**; records are confidential
• Emphasise a **non-judgemental** approach
• Offer a **chaperone for all intimate examinations**; accommodate requests for a clinician of a particular gender
• Start with **open questions**, then closed questions
• Be **explicit**; avoid unclear terms and clarify slang the patient uses
• Watch for anxiety and **non-verbal cues**
cards.m: Open first, explicit always, judge never.

cards.q: Which STI screening tests are recommended for a heterosexual man (symptomatic or asymptomatic)?
cards.a:
• **Blood**: HIV Ag/Ab, syphilis serology (RPR/VDRL **plus** TPPA/TPHA/CMIA/ECLIA)
• **HBsAg and anti-HCV** if blood-borne virus risk
• **Urine (first pass)**: chlamydia/gonorrhoea (CT/NG) **NAAT**
cards.m: One blood tube for the 4 viruses/syphilis, one pot of first-pass urine for CT/NG.

cards.q: What counts as blood-borne virus (BBV) risk, triggering hepatitis B and C testing?
cards.a:
• Unprotected sex with an **HIV-positive** person or with **MSM**
• **Chemsex** or group sex
• **Injecting drug use** (self or partner)
• **Sharing straws/paper rolls** for snorting drugs
• **Paid for or been paid for sex**
• Medical treatment or **tattooing** where sterility is not guaranteed

cards.q: What is the preferred specimen for chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT in men and in women?
cards.a:
• **Men**: **first-pass urine** (as or more sensitive than a urethral swab, and more acceptable)
• **Women**: **self-collected vulvovaginal swab** (specimen of choice)
• Endocervical swab if a speculum examination is being done
• Female first-pass urine only if swabs cannot be taken
cards.m: Men pee, women swab.

cards.q: Which extra-genital samples should be taken in MSM and in women, and when?
cards.a:
• **Pharyngeal swab** CT/NG NAAT if **receptive oral sex**
• **Rectal swab** CT/NG NAAT if **receptive anal sex**
• Extra-genital sampling should be **routine in all MSM**; in others guided by risk and symptoms
• Samples may be **pooled** for testing
cards.m: Sample every orifice that was used.

cards.q: How should STI screening be approached in women who have sex with women (WSW) and in transgender people?
cards.a:
• **WSW**: no routine testing unless **symptomatic or reporting sex with men**; ask explicitly about sex with men
• **Transgender**: screen according to **sexual behaviour**, as for cisgender people
• **Transmen with a vagina** (vaginal sex): **vaginal swab** rather than urine
• **Transwomen with neovagina**: **urine** preferred over vaginal swab
• Anyone with receptive anal sex: **rectal swab**

cards.q: What are the window periods for the common STI tests?
cards.a:
• **Chlamydia NAAT**: 2 weeks
• **Gonorrhoea NAAT**: 2 weeks
• **HIV Ag/Ab**: 4 weeks
• **Syphilis serology**: 6–12 weeks
• **Hepatitis B**: 3–6 months
• **Hepatitis C**: up to 6 months
cards.m: 2-2-4 then 6-12 weeks, then months for the hepatitis viruses.

cards.q: A known contact of an STI tests negative while still inside the window period. What does the guideline advise?
cards.a:
• A negative test inside the window period does **not exclude** infection
• **Offer re-testing** after the window period
• **Consider (epidemiological) treatment** now if the person is a known contact
cards.m: Window period = blind period: treat the contact, retest later.

cards.q: In the symptomatic male consultation template, why ask when he last passed urine?
cards.a:
• Ideally **more than 2 hours** since last void
• Allows discharge to accumulate for **urethral smear/milking** and improves first-pass urine yield
• Template also records chaperone name, specimens taken and urethral/rectal Gram stain findings

cards.q: Which genital symptoms should be specifically asked about in the symptom review, by sex?
cards.a:
• **Male**: urethral discharge, dysuria, genital skin problems, testicular pain/swelling, ejaculatory problems, peri-anal/anal symptoms (MSM)
• **Female**: unusual vaginal discharge, vulval skin problems, lower abdominal pain/**deep dyspareunia**, dysuria, **intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding**

cards.q: Which STIs are notifiable in Malaysia, under which law, and how quickly?
cards.a:
• **Syphilis, gonorrhoea, HIV and chancroid** (4 of the 31 notifiable diseases)
• **Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases Act 1988 (Act 342)**
• Notify the nearest **District Health Office within 7 days** of diagnosis (e-notification/phone/form)
• Failure to notify can be compounded under the Act
cards.m: Notify the 'S-G-H-C' four: Syphilis, Gonorrhoea, HIV, Chancroid.

cards.q: For syphilis notification, which cases must be notified – acquired vs congenital?
cards.a:
• **Acquired syphilis**: **only confirmed** cases (stage may be stated on the form)
• **Congenital syphilis**: **probable, confirmed and syphilitic stillbirths** are all notified
• Gonorrhoea and HIV: confirmed cases only
• All within **7 days** to the District Health Office

cards.q: What is partner notification, and which method is supported by evidence?
cards.a:
• Contacting sexual partners of an index patient to offer **screening and treatment**
• Aims: interrupt transmission, prevent **re-infection** and complications
• **Patient referral** (index patient tells partners) is effective and **less labour-intensive and costly** than provider referral
• Depends on **confidentiality**; beware risk of **violence** against the index case (especially women)
• Offer both methods and **document** the one agreed

cards.q: Why is it a public-health priority to treat an STI at the patient's FIRST encounter?
cards.a:
• Both **ulcerative and non-ulcerative STIs increase sexual HIV transmission**
• Prevents complications (PID, infertility, congenital infection)
• Reduces onward spread in the community
• Offers a unique chance for **HIV screening and prevention education**
• Malaysian syphilis incidence nearly doubled (5.7 to 14.3 per 100,000, 2012–2022), mostly men aged 20–39
cards.m: Every STI visit is an HIV-prevention visit.

cards.q: What is the Modified Syndromic Approach (MSA) and how does it differ from aetiological management?
cards.a:
• STIs with similar symptoms/signs are grouped into **syndromes**
• In MSA, **empirical treatment is given at the first visit** to cover likely pathogens
• At follow-up, **lab results are traced** to confirm the pathogen, **modify treatment** and assess response
• Aetiological management waits for a lab diagnosis before treating
cards.m: MSA = treat today, confirm tomorrow.

cards.q: Name the five syndromes used in the Malaysian Modified Syndromic Approach.
cards.a:
• **Anogenital ulcer** disease syndrome
• **Urethral discharge** syndrome
• **Vaginal discharge** syndrome
• **Lower abdominal pain** syndrome
• **Anorectal discharge** syndrome
cards.m: U-U-V-L-A: Ulcer, Urethra, Vagina, Lower abdomen, Anus.

cards.q: What are the two main limitations of syndromic management?
cards.a:
• **Poor sensitivity and specificity for cervical infection** in women (gonococcal/chlamydial cervicitis), even where STI prevalence is high
• **Over-diagnosis and over-treatment** of patients with no or only one infection (cost, resistance)
• By contrast it performs well for **urethral discharge** and **genital ulcer** syndromes
cards.m: Good for the penis and the ulcer, poor for the cervix.

cards.q: In the anogenital ulcer flowchart, which clinical pattern points to which infection?
cards.a:
• **Single painless ulcer** (± nodes) → **primary syphilis**
• **Multiple painful vesicles** ± shallow ulcers → **genital herpes**
• **Painful ulcers**, necrotic base, purulent, ragged undermined edges, **painful buboes** → **chancroid**
• **Painless ulcer + proctitis**/discharge + painful lymphadenitis/buboes → **LGV**
cards.m: Syphilis is the silent sore; chancroid is the crying sore.

cards.q: Anogenital ulcer present: what is done at the first visit and when is review?
cards.a:
• **Syphilis RDT, RPR, TPPA**, NAAT if available
• Screen for **HIV, hepatitis B and C**
• **Same-day treatment** per the ulcer table
• Educate, counsel, provide condoms
• **Epidemiological treatment for partners** if syphilis, LGV or chancroid
• **Return in 7 days**; if not healed and not improving → **refer dermatologist/ID physician**
cards.m: Ulcers come back in a week.

cards.q: What is the preferred empirical treatment for urethral discharge syndrome?
cards.a:
• **Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT** (1g if body weight >150kg) for gonorrhoea
• **PLUS doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 7 days** for chlamydia
• Plus education, condoms, HIV/hepatitis/syphilis screening and **partner epidemiological treatment**
cards.m: Two bugs, two drugs: Ceftriaxone for the Gonococcus, Doxy for the Chlamydia.

cards.q: Urethral or cervical discharge: what are the alternative and pregnancy regimens?
cards.a:
• **Alternative**: **gentamicin 240mg IM STAT PLUS azithromycin 2g PO STAT**
• **Pregnancy**: **ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT PLUS azithromycin 1g PO STAT**
• Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy, hence azithromycin
cards.m: Azithro dose: 2g when it must also cover gonorrhoea (with gentamicin), 1g when it only covers chlamydia.

cards.q: Urethral discharge syndrome: how is discharge confirmed, and when is the man reviewed?
cards.a:
• Examine and **milk the urethra** if discharge is not obvious
• Gram stain/culture and sensitivity/NAAT if available
• **Notify** once laboratory confirmed (gonorrhoea)
• **Return in 14 days**

cards.q: A man returns with persistent/recurrent urethral discharge after standard treatment. What is the logic of the flowchart?
cards.a:
• Confirm discharge (milk urethra)
• **Re-infection or poor compliance?** → **repeat** standard urethral discharge treatment
• If not → treat for **Trichomonas vaginalis and Mycoplasma genitalium**
• Partner epidemiological treatment; **return in 7 days** if symptoms persist
• Not improved → **refer dermatologist/ID physician**
cards.m: Persistent discharge: think re-exposure first, then 'T and M' (Trich and Myco).

cards.q: What is the regimen for resistant or persistent urethral discharge?
cards.a:
• **Metronidazole 400mg PO q12h for 5 days** (T. vaginalis)
• **PLUS** for M. genitalium:
• – if **doxycycline** was first line → **azithromycin 500mg STAT, then 250mg daily for 4 days**
• – if **azithromycin** was first line → **moxifloxacin 400mg daily for 10–14 days**
cards.m: Switch class: after doxy give azithro; after azithro give moxi.

cards.q: Vaginal discharge without speculum examination (risk-assessment flowchart): what same-day treatment is given?
cards.a:
• Covers **candidiasis and bacterial vaginosis** based on discharge characteristics
• **Clotrimazole 500mg vaginal pessary STAT** (alternative fluconazole 150–200mg PO STAT)
• **PLUS metronidazole 400mg PO q12h for 5–7 days** (alternatives clindamycin 300mg q12h 7 days or metronidazole 2g STAT)
• Pregnancy: clotrimazole pessary + metronidazole 400mg q12h 5–7 days
• Screen HIV/hepatitis/syphilis; **return in 14 days**

cards.q: Speculum-based vaginal discharge flowchart: what findings decide the treatment?
cards.a:
• **Lower abdominal or cervical motion tenderness** → lower abdominal pain (PID) flowchart
• **Cervical mucopurulent discharge** → same-day treatment for **gonorrhoea + chlamydia**, partner treatment, notify
• **Vulval oedema, curd-like discharge or erythema** → treat **candidiasis + BV**
• None of these → consider alternative diagnosis and refer
• Return in **14 days**
cards.m: Pus from the cervix = GC/CT; curds on the vulva = Candida.

cards.q: Lower abdominal pain syndrome: which findings mandate referral for surgical/gynaecological assessment?
cards.a:
• **Pregnant** or **missed/overdue period**
• **Recent delivery, abortion or miscarriage**
• **Guarding and/or rebound tenderness**
• **Abnormal vaginal bleeding**
• **Abdominal mass**
• **Abnormal vital signs**
• Set up an **IV line and resuscitate** before transfer
cards.m: Rule out ectopic, sepsis and the surgical abdomen before calling it PID.

cards.q: Lower abdominal pain syndrome with no red flags: when is PID treated and when reviewed?
cards.a:
• If **cervical excitation tenderness**, or **lower abdominal tenderness with vaginal discharge** → **manage as PID**
• **Review in 3 days**
• Improved → complete treatment, educate, condoms, offer HIV/hepatitis/syphilis screening
• Not improved → **refer gynaecologist**

cards.q: Who enters the anorectal discharge syndrome flowchart and what is the first-visit treatment?
cards.a:
• **Passive (receptive) anal sex in the last 6 months** and/or anal symptoms
• If anal discharge: rectal Gram stain/culture/NAAT
• **Same-day treatment for gonorrhoea and chlamydia**: ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT **plus** doxycycline 100mg q12h 7 days
• **Return in 7 days**

cards.q: Anorectal discharge persists at the 7-day review, or the patient has anal pain with an ulcer. What next?
cards.a:
• **Persistent rectal discharge** → **consider treating for LGV**: doxycycline 100mg q12h for **21 days** (alternatives azithromycin 1g weekly for 3 weeks, or erythromycin 800mg q6h 21 days)
• **Anal/perianal pain with ulcer** → consider treating for **herpes simplex**
cards.m: Proctitis that won't settle in MSM = LGV until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Which STIs can be fully treated through the syndromic approach?
cards.a:
• **Syphilis**
• **Gonorrhoea**
• **Chlamydia**
• **Trichomoniasis**
• **Candidiasis**
• (Viral STIs – HSV, HPV, HIV – can be managed but not cured)

cards.q: What causes syphilis and how is acquired syphilis classified?
cards.a:
• **Treponema pallidum** subspecies pallidum
• **Early syphilis (<2 years)**: primary, secondary, early latent
• **Late syphilis (>2 years or unknown duration)**: late latent, tertiary (gumma, cardiovascular, neurosyphilis)
• Congenital: early (<2 years old) and late (>2 years old)
cards.m: The 2-year rule splits early from late – and 'unknown' counts as late.

cards.q: Why does a syphilis diagnosis need two kinds of serological test?
cards.a:
• **Non-treponemal** (RPR/VDRL): detect cardiolipin antibodies; **quantitative titre reflects disease activity**; used to **stage, decide treatment and monitor response**; can be **biologically false positive**
• **Treponemal** (TPPA/TPHA/CMIA/ECLIA/RDT): specific; confirm exposure; **usually stay positive for life**, so **not used to monitor treatment**
cards.m: RPR = Report on Present Rate of disease; TPPA = Treponemes Previously, Persists Always.

cards.q: Describe the 'traditional' syphilis screening algorithm and its interpretations.
cards.a:
• Start with **RPR**; if reactive → **TPPA**
• RPR non-reactive → syphilis unlikely without risk; repeat in 2–4 weeks if indicated
• **RPR reactive + TPPA positive** → syphilis (treated or untreated)
• **RPR reactive + TPPA negative** → syphilis unlikely; **possible biological false positive**; repeat in 2–4 weeks if at risk

cards.q: Describe the 'reverse' syphilis screening algorithm.
cards.a:
• Start with an automated **treponemal test (CMIA/ECLIA)**
• Reactive → **RPR**: reactive = consistent with syphilis (past or current)
• **CMIA reactive, RPR non-reactive** → do **TPPA** (check for a previous TPPA first)
• TPPA positive → suggestive of syphilis (previously treated or untreated)
• TPPA negative → syphilis unlikely (false-positive CMIA); repeat 2–4 weeks if at risk
cards.m: Reverse = Treponemal first; TPPA is the tie-breaker.

cards.q: How does the rapid diagnostic test (RDT) algorithm work at primary care?
cards.a:
• **RDT** (treponemal) at point of care
• **Positive** → **refer FMS/physician/MO** and send **RPR**
• RPR reactive → consistent with syphilis (past or current)
• RPR non-reactive → **treponemal test (CMIA/ECLIA) or TPPA**: positive = suggestive of syphilis; negative = unlikely
• RDT negative → syphilis unlikely without high-risk exposure

cards.q: What is the prozone phenomenon in syphilis serology?
cards.a:
• A **false-negative (or weakly reactive) non-treponemal test** caused by a **very high antibody titre** that blocks lattice formation
• Typical in **secondary syphilis**, pregnancy and HIV
• Suspect when clinical picture is florid but RPR is negative/weak
• Ask the lab to **repeat RPR on diluted serum**; treponemal test will be positive
cards.m: Too many antibodies, no clump – dilute to see the lump.

cards.q: Primary syphilis: incubation period and classic lesion?
cards.a:
• Incubation **9–90 days**
• **Chancre**: **solitary, painless (non-tender), indurated**, well-circumscribed ulcer
• **Regional lymphadenopathy** (rubbery, non-tender)
• Atypical: multiple, painful, purulent or **extragenital (most often oral)**; syphilitic balanitis of Follmann
• Anal, oral or cervical chancres often go unnoticed
• **Any anogenital ulcer is syphilis until proven otherwise**
cards.m: Chancre = 'hard, harmless-feeling, hidden' – painless so patients ignore it.

cards.q: A patient has a typical chancre but negative syphilis serology. What does the guideline advise?
cards.a:
• Serology may not yet have turned positive in early primary syphilis
• Give **presumptive treatment**
• **Repeat serology after 2 weeks**
• Consider a **T. pallidum PCR swab** of the lesion
cards.m: A chancre can beat the antibodies – treat, swab, retest.

cards.q: Where is T. pallidum PCR useful?
cards.a:
• Demonstrates **T. pallidum directly** in lesion swabs and **tissue samples**
• Also **vitreous fluid** (ocular syphilis) and **CSF**
• Useful in **seronegative early primary** syphilis and for gumma tissue
• (Dark-field microscopy of exudate is the classic direct method in case definitions)

cards.q: Secondary syphilis: incubation and commonest presentation?
cards.a:
• Incubation **6 weeks – 6 months**
• Commonest: **generalised non-itchy rash involving the palms and soles** ± generalised lymphadenopathy
• Less common: **condylomata lata**, mucocutaneous (snail-track) lesions, **patchy ('moth-eaten') alopecia**
• Rash may be itchy in dark-skinned patients
• The primary chancre may still be present
cards.m: A rash on the palms and soles in a sexually active adult = secondary syphilis until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Why can secondary syphilis present to almost any specialty?
cards.a:
• It is the **bacteraemic stage** – haematogenous dissemination
• **Eye**: anterior uveitis
• **CNS**: meningitis, cranial nerve palsies
• **Liver/spleen**: hepatitis, splenomegaly
• **Bone**: periostitis
• **Kidney**: glomerulonephritis
• Plus fever, malaise, myalgia, pharyngitis
cards.m: Secondary syphilis – 'the great imitator'.

cards.q: What serology results are expected in untreated secondary syphilis?
cards.a:
• **All serological tests are positive** (treponemal and non-treponemal)
• **RPR/VDRL titre usually >1:8**
• A negative or weak RPR with florid signs → think **prozone**, ask for dilution

cards.q: Define early latent syphilis.
cards.a:
• **Positive serology without symptoms or signs**
• In a person known to be **seronegative within the previous 2 years**
• Case-definition clues: a fourfold titre rise within 24 months, or untreated symptoms/exposure to early syphilis within 24 months
• No such evidence = **late latent**
cards.m: Latent = serology only; early if you can prove it began within 2 years.

cards.q: First-line treatment of early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent) in a non-pregnant adult?
cards.a:
• **Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM STAT** (single dose)
• OR procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for 10 days
• **Penicillin allergy**: **doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 14 days**
• Warn about the **Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction**
• **Abstain from sex until 1 week after** patient and partner(s) complete treatment
cards.m: Early = one shot (2.4MU once); late = three shots.

cards.q: How far back should partners be traced for each stage of early syphilis?
cards.a:
• **Primary**: **3 months** plus duration of symptoms (or since last negative test)
• **Secondary**: **6 months** plus duration of symptoms (or last negative test)
• **Early latent**: **12 months** (or most recent negative test)
• Late latent: test current partner(s); if unsure early vs late, trace as early latent
cards.m: 3-6-12: Primary, Secondary, Early latent.

cards.q: Which sexual contacts of a patient with early syphilis are treated epidemiologically, and with what?
cards.a:
• Contact **<90 days** before diagnosis → **treat for early syphilis even if serology is negative**
• Contact **>90 days** → treat if serology is **not immediately available and follow-up uncertain**
• Positive serology → treat according to stage
• Regimen: **benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM STAT** (allergy: doxycycline 100mg q12h 14 days)
• Recommended for asymptomatic contacts **including pregnant women** (after counselling)
cards.m: Within 90 days the contact may be incubating – serology can't see it yet.

cards.q: Define late latent syphilis and what must be done at diagnosis.
cards.a:
• Syphilis of **more than 2 years or unknown duration**
• **Positive serology without symptoms**
• Do a **thorough clinical examination** to exclude **cardiovascular and neurological** involvement

cards.q: Treatment of late latent, gummatous or cardiovascular syphilis in a non-pregnant adult?
cards.a:
• **Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 weeks (3 doses)**
• OR procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for **14 days**
• Penicillin allergy: **doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 28 days**
• Cardiovascular syphilis: consider **prednisolone 40–60mg daily for 3 days, starting 24 hours before** antibiotics
cards.m: Late syphilis doubles everything: 3 doses instead of 1, 28 days doxy instead of 14.

cards.q: A patient on weekly benzathine penicillin for late latent syphilis misses a dose. When must the course restart?
cards.a:
• If the gap between weekly doses is **2 weeks or more**, the **whole 3-dose regimen must be restarted**
• Shorter delays: continue the course
cards.m: Benzathine levels last about 3 weeks – a 2-week gap breaks the chain.

cards.q: Gumma and cardiovascular syphilis: incubation and features?
cards.a:
• **Gumma**: incubation **1–45 years (average 15)**; destructive **granulomatous** lesion of **skin or bone** (also liver, heart, brain); PCR on tissue
• **Cardiovascular**: incubation **15–30 years**; **aortitis of the proximal aorta** → **aortic regurgitation** (± heart failure), **coronary ostial stenosis** (angina), **aortic aneurysm**
• Investigate CV syphilis with **CXR and echocardiogram**

cards.q: When is syphilis considered a treatment failure, and what is done?
cards.a:
• **Signs/symptoms persist or recur**, OR
• **RPR fails to fall fourfold by 1 year**, OR
• **Sustained fourfold or greater rise** in RPR
• Exclude reinfection, then do **CSF examination**
• Neurosyphilis excluded → **benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 weeks**
cards.m: Failure = no 4-fold fall in a year, or a 4-fold rise any time.

cards.q: Ocular syphilis and otosyphilis: key facts?
cards.a:
• Can occur at **any stage**, commonly early
• **Ocular**: most often **panuveitis**; also conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis, interstitial keratitis, optic neuropathy, retinal vasculitis → risk of **permanent vision loss**
• **Otosyphilis**: tinnitus, vertigo, **sensorineural hearing loss** (sudden, unilateral or bilateral, rapidly progressive)
• Ocular symptoms + reactive serology → full eye exam incl. cranial nerves; **CSF if cranial nerve dysfunction**
• Treated as **neurosyphilis**

cards.q: What are the CSF criteria for neurosyphilis?
cards.a:
• **WBC**: >5/µL if **HIV negative**; >20/µL if HIV positive (or 6–20/µL if on ART, viral load undetectable, CD4 >200)
• **Protein >0.45 g/L**
• **CSF VDRL positive**
• A **negative CSF VDRL makes neurosyphilis unlikely but does not exclude it**
cards.m: CSF VDRL: highly specific, poorly sensitive.

cards.q: Compare meningovascular and parenchymatous neurosyphilis.
cards.a:
• **Meningovascular**: incubation **5–10 years**; headache, vertigo, **cranial nerve palsies**, stroke
• **Parenchymatous**: incubation **10–20 years**
• – **General paresis** (brain): gradual **personality change**, ataxia, stroke, eye signs
• – **Tabes dorsalis** (cord): **lightning pains**, sensory loss, gait/mobility problems
• Both are differentials of **dementia, psychiatric illness and falls**
cards.m: Check syphilis serology in new dementia or psychosis.

cards.q: Treatment of neurosyphilis (including ocular/otosyphilis)?
cards.a:
• **Benzylpenicillin 4MU IV q4h for 14 days**
• OR **procaine penicillin 2.4MU IM daily + probenecid 500mg PO q6h**, both for 14 days
• Allergy **without anaphylaxis**: **ceftriaxone 2g IM/IV daily for 14 days**
• **Anaphylaxis** to penicillin: **doxycycline 200mg PO q12h for 28 days**
• Consider **prednisolone 40–60mg daily for 3 days**, starting 24h before antibiotics
cards.m: Benzathine does not reach the CSF reliably – neurosyphilis needs IV benzylpenicillin.

cards.q: Follow-up after treatment of any stage of syphilis?
cards.a:
• Clinical review + **RPR titre at 3, 6 and 12 months**
• **Fourfold fall** (e.g. **1:8 → 1:2**, two dilutions) = **adequate response**
• Then RPR **every 6 months** until **negative or serofast**
• Treponemal tests (TPPA/CMIA) are **not** used – they stay positive
cards.m: Four-fold = two tube dilutions.

cards.q: What is a serofast state?
cards.a:
• After adequate treatment and an appropriate fall, the RPR **stays low-titre reactive and stable** (e.g. ≤1:4) rather than becoming negative
• Not treatment failure if titre is low and **stable** and there is no clinical relapse
• A **sustained fourfold rise** from the serofast level suggests **reinfection or relapse**

cards.q: Describe the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR).
cards.a:
• Acute febrile reaction: **fever, headache, malaise, rigors, joint pains**
• Starts **6–12 hours after treatment**, resolves **within 24 hours**
• **Common in early syphilis**; usually unimportant except with **neurological/ophthalmic** involvement or in **pregnancy** (**foetal distress, premature labour**)
• Uncommon in late syphilis but **potentially life-threatening at strategic sites** (coronary ostia, larynx, CNS)
• Managed with **antipyretics**; it is not penicillin allergy
cards.m: JHR = dying treponemes release toxins – fever the same day, gone by tomorrow.

cards.q: When should pregnant women be screened for syphilis?
cards.a:
• **First antenatal visit (booking)**
• **Repeat at 28–32 weeks** (high-risk women)
• **Late bookers (≥28 weeks)** or unbooked: screen at presentation, repeat **within 1 month**
• Any woman with a **foetal death after 20 weeks** must be tested
• Test with RPR/VDRL or **RDT**; confirm as for non-pregnant adults
cards.m: Book, then 28–32: two chances to catch it before the baby does.

cards.q: An antenatal mother at a Klinik Kesihatan has a positive syphilis RDT. What happens at that visit?
cards.a:
• Health education and **informed consent**
• Refer to the **FMS/MO** to **start treatment (1st dose benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM) the same day**
• **AND send blood for RPR** (then TPPA/CMIA if RPR non-reactive)
• Notify, **contact-trace and treat the partner**
• Refer to hospital specialist (O&G/dermatologist/ID) for further management and delivery
cards.m: Positive RDT in pregnancy: needle first, paperwork later (WHO 'Strategy C').

cards.q: Which antenatal mothers need the 2nd and 3rd weekly doses of benzathine penicillin?
cards.a:
• **Late latent** syphilis
• **Unknown duration** of infection
• Previously treated syphilis **more than 2 years ago** with a **current fourfold rise in titre**
• Early syphilis: the single dose suffices

cards.q: Treatment of early syphilis in pregnancy and in the penicillin-allergic pregnant woman?
cards.a:
• **Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM STAT** (or procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for 10 days)
• **Penicillin allergy → desensitise and treat with penicillin** (no proven alternatives)
• If desensitisation fails: ceftriaxone 500mg IM daily for 10 days OR azithromycin 2g PO STAT
• **Doxycycline/tetracycline is contraindicated** in pregnancy

cards.q: Why must a penicillin-allergic pregnant woman with syphilis be desensitised rather than given an alternative?
cards.a:
• **Penicillin G is the only known effective antimicrobial for preventing transmission to the foetus and treating foetal infection**
• Macrolides cross the placenta poorly and resistance occurs; doxycycline is contraindicated
• Benefit outweighs the risk of skin testing and desensitisation
• If a **macrolide or other non-penicillin** regimen is used → the **neonate must be assessed and treated at birth**
cards.m: Only penicillin protects the passenger.

cards.q: How is a pregnant woman followed up after syphilis treatment?
cards.a:
• Advise to seek care if **change in foetal movements or contractions** after treatment (JHR → foetal distress/preterm labour)
• **Monthly clinical and serological review until delivery**
• **Repeat RPR at delivery** (and test the baby at the same time for comparison)
• Thereafter follow-up as non-pregnant adults

cards.q: In which patients is oral penicillin desensitisation ABSOLUTELY contraindicated?
cards.a:
• **Poorly controlled asthma** (FEV1 <70% predicted)
• **Unstable vital signs**
• **Uncontrolled active cardiac disease**
• History of penicillin-induced **SJS/TEN, DRESS** or immuno-cytotoxic reactions
• **Non-IgE** reactions (fixed drug eruption, maculopapular rash, erythema multiforme, vasculitis)
• These patients get alternatives, and their **newborns need IV penicillin immediately after delivery**
cards.m: Desensitisation only works for IgE allergy – it cannot switch off SJS.

cards.q: What precautions apply when desensitising a pregnant woman to penicillin?
cards.a:
• Done by an experienced clinician in **HDU/ICU**
• **Obstetric team on standby** and **foetal monitoring**
• **IV access**, regular vital signs, anaphylaxis drugs at bedside
• Withhold non-selective **β-blockers** 24h before/after; skip morning **ACE inhibitor**
• Informed consent
• Adverse events include **uterine contractions** (miscarriage risk) and **JHR**

cards.q: After successful desensitisation for the first benzathine dose, how are the 2nd and 3rd weekly doses given?
cards.a:
• As **regular injections** – benzathine's long half-life keeps levels up to 3 weeks
• As a precaution: admit, give a **test dose of penicillin V 400,000 units PO**, observe 1 hour
• No reaction → **benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM**, monitor overnight
• If doses are separated by more than **2–5 half-lives**, the **whole desensitisation must be repeated**

cards.q: How is anaphylaxis to penicillin treated?
cards.a:
• **Adrenaline 0.5mg IM STAT** (repeat every 3–5 min as needed)
• ± **hydrocortisone** IV/IM and **chlorpheniramine 10mg IM**
• Lie flat, legs raised, oxygen, IV fluids 20 ml/kg if hypotensive
• Facilities for anaphylaxis must be available wherever penicillin is given
cards.m: Adrenaline in the thigh, half a milligram, without delay.

cards.q: What are the WHO EMTCT targets for syphilis, and what is Malaysia's status?
cards.a:
• **≥95% antenatal care** coverage (≥1 visit)
• **≥95% syphilis testing** of pregnant women
• **≥95% treatment** (≥1 dose IM benzathine penicillin **≥30 days before delivery**)
• Goal: congenital syphilis **≤50 per 100,000 live births**
• **Malaysia (2018): first in the Western Pacific Region certified for EMTCT of HIV and syphilis**
cards.m: Three 95s and a 50.

cards.q: What counts as ADEQUATE maternal treatment when assessing a syphilis-exposed baby?
cards.a:
• At least **one injection of benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM**
• Given **at least 30 days before delivery**
• With a regimen **appropriate for stage** and an expected RPR fall
• Inadequate: untreated, **non-penicillin regimen** (e.g. erythromycin), treatment **<30 days** before delivery, poor serological follow-up
cards.m: Penicillin, plus 30 days, plus falling titre.

cards.q: Clinical features of early congenital syphilis (child under 2 years)?
cards.a:
• **Rash** (incl. palms/soles, desquamation) and **snuffles** (rhinitis)
• **Hepatosplenomegaly**, **jaundice** (non-viral hepatitis/cholestasis)
• **Condylomata lata**
• **Pseudoparalysis** (painful osteochondritis)
• **Anaemia**, **oedema** (nephrotic syndrome), non-immune hydrops
cards.m: Snuffles + rash + big liver + won't move a limb.

cards.q: Stigmata of late congenital syphilis (older child)?
cards.a:
• **Interstitial keratitis**, **nerve deafness**, **Hutchinson teeth** (Hutchinson triad)
• **Mulberry molars**
• **Frontal bossing**, **saddle nose**
• **Anterior bowing of the shins** (sabre tibia)
• **Rhagades** (perioral fissure scars)
• **Clutton joints** (painless knee effusions)
cards.m: Hutchinson triad: Eyes (keratitis), Ears (deafness), Enamel (notched incisors).

cards.q: Which infants born to seropositive mothers must be evaluated for congenital syphilis?
cards.a:
Mothers who:
• had **untreated** syphilis
• were treated **less than 1 month before delivery**
• were treated with a **non-penicillin** regimen
• **did not show the expected RPR fall** after treatment
• had **insufficient serological follow-up** in pregnancy

cards.q: What does evaluation of an at-risk infant for congenital syphilis include?
cards.a:
• **Thorough physical examination**
• **Infant RPR compared with mother's RPR at delivery**
• **CSF**: cells, protein, CSF-VDRL
• **Long-bone X-rays** (osteochondritis, periostitis)
• **Chest X-ray**
• Older infants: also FBC, LFT, eye exam, hearing, neuroimaging; screen for **HIV**

cards.q: Which findings make congenital syphilis 'highly probable'?
cards.a:
• **Abnormal examination** consistent with congenital syphilis, OR
• Infant RPR **≥ fourfold higher than mother's** at delivery (e.g. mother 1:8, baby ≥1:32), OR
• Mother **untreated or inadequately treated** at delivery (regardless of signs), OR
• Reactive RPR **plus** abnormal long-bone X-ray, reactive CSF-VDRL or raised CSF WBC/protein

cards.q: Congenital syphilis 'less likely' vs 'unlikely': how do they differ and how are they managed?
cards.a:
Both: normal exam, infant titre ≤ fourfold of mother's
• **Less likely**: mother treated **during pregnancy**, stage-appropriate, **≥30 days before delivery**, no reinfection → no evaluation; **benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg IM single dose**
• **Unlikely**: mother adequately treated **before pregnancy**, titre low and stable (**VDRL ≤1:2, RPR ≤1:4**) → **no treatment**; follow serology until negative (benzathine may be considered if follow-up uncertain)

cards.q: Preferred treatment of confirmed/highly probable congenital syphilis in a neonate?
cards.a:
• **Benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg/dose IV q12h for the first 7 days of life, then q8h** to complete **10 days**
• OR procaine penicillin 50,000 units/kg IM daily for 10–14 days
• Alternative: ceftriaxone 75mg/kg IM daily (<30 days old) or 100mg/kg (≥30 days), 10–14 days
• If treatment is interrupted **≥1 day**, **restart the whole course**
• Needs evaluation but follow-up uncertain → **benzathine penicillin 50,000 units/kg IM STAT**

cards.q: How are seropositive infants followed up, and what RPR trend is expected?
cards.a:
• **Untreated** seropositive infants: review at **1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 months**
• Passively acquired RPR should **fall by 3 months and usually disappear by 6 months**
• Treat if signs persist/recur, **RPR rises fourfold** by 3 months, **RPR still positive at 6 months**, or TPHA positive at 1 year
• **Treated** infants: review at 1, 3, 6, 12, 18 and 24 months; repeat LP 6-monthly until normal
cards.m: Maternal antibody fades by 6 months; the baby's own infection doesn't.

cards.q: Gonorrhoea: organism and incubation period by sex?
cards.a:
• **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** – Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus
• Incubation **1–14 days**
• **Men** usually symptomatic within **2–5 days**
• **Women** within **10 days** – but many women are asymptomatic

cards.q: Typical presentations of gonorrhoea in men and women?
cards.a:
• **Men**: **purulent urethral discharge**, dysuria; epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, balanitis; **proctitis** after receptive anal sex
• **Women**: often asymptomatic; non-specific vaginal discharge (mucopurulent cervicitis), dysuria, **intermenstrual/post-coital bleeding**, dyspareunia, lower abdominal pain/PID
• Pharyngeal infection usually asymptomatic
cards.m: Gonorrhoea is the 'drip' – thick, yellow and quick (2–5 days).

cards.q: List the complications of gonorrhoea.
cards.a:
• **PID → ectopic pregnancy, infertility**
• **Bartholin** and other accessory gland abscess
• **Disseminated gonococcal infection** (skin pustules, arthritis, tenosynovitis, endocarditis, meningitis)
• **Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome)**
• Gonococcal conjunctivitis, **ophthalmia neonatorum**
• Periurethral abscess/fistula, **urethral stricture**, perianal abscess

cards.q: How useful is a Gram stain for gonorrhoea in men vs women?
cards.a:
• Finding: **intracellular Gram-negative diplococci within polymorphs**
• **Symptomatic men** (urethral): sensitivity **~95%**, specificity 99% – can be diagnostic
• **Asymptomatic men**: 50–75%
• **Women** (cervical): sensitivity only **45–65%** – a negative smear does not exclude infection
cards.m: Gram stain: great for the dripping penis, poor for the cervix.

cards.q: NAAT vs culture for gonorrhoea – what does each offer?
cards.a:
• **NAAT**: sensitivity **>95%** in symptomatic and asymptomatic infection; **more sensitive than culture**; self-collected swabs OK
• **Culture**: still the **gold standard**; the only way to get **antimicrobial susceptibility** and monitor resistance
• Anyone diagnosed by NAAT should have **cultures from infected sites before treatment** – but **do not delay treatment** for results
cards.m: NAAT finds it, culture fights resistance.

cards.q: What are the practical requirements for gonococcal culture?
cards.a:
• Clinician must **specifically request 'gonococcal culture'**
• Selective media (**Modified Thayer-Martin** or GC agar), incubated in **increased CO2**
• Specimen must **reach the lab within 24 hours**
• Sites: urethral, endocervical, neovaginal, anorectal, pharyngeal

cards.q: First-line treatment of uncomplicated urogenital or anorectal gonorrhoea?
cards.a:
• **Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT** (**1g if weight >150kg**)
• Alternative (e.g. cephalosporin allergy): **gentamicin 240mg IM STAT AND azithromycin 2g PO STAT**
• **Pharyngeal** gonorrhoea: discuss with an expert (harder to eradicate)
• Plus chlamydia cover if not excluded
cards.m: Gonorrhoea = one jab of ceftriaxone 500.

cards.q: When gonorrhoea is treated, when and how is chlamydia also covered?
cards.a:
• If chlamydia **has not been ruled out** (e.g. NAAT pending)
• **Non-pregnant**: **doxycycline 100mg PO BD for 7 days**
• **Pregnant**: **azithromycin 1g PO single dose**

cards.q: How are gonococcal conjunctivitis and disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) treated in adults?
cards.a:
• **Conjunctivitis**: **ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT** + consider one-time **saline lavage**; **refer ophthalmologist**
• **DGI**: hospitalise; **ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV daily**
• – Arthritis-dermatitis: **≥7 days**
• – Meningitis: **10–14 days**
• – Endocarditis: **4 weeks**
cards.m: DGI durations 1-2-4: one week joints/skin, two weeks brain, four weeks heart.

cards.q: Partner management and sexual advice after a gonorrhoea diagnosis?
cards.a:
• Partners **within the last 60 days**: **treat epidemiologically regardless of test results**
• Partners before 60 days: evaluate and treat if necessary
• **Newborns of infected mothers must be screened**
• Abstain from condomless sex for **7 days after both are treated** and symptoms resolve
• Notify confirmed cases
cards.m: 60 days look-back for GC, CT, NGU, PID, LGV and donovanosis.

cards.q: When is a test of cure recommended for gonorrhoea?
cards.a:
• **Pharyngeal** gonorrhoea
• Treated with **anything other than the first-line regimen** when susceptibility is unknown
• Done **7–14 days after treatment** (culture or NAAT)
• **Not routine** for uncomplicated cervical, urethral or rectal infection treated with ceftriaxone
• **Persistent symptoms** → culture with susceptibility testing

cards.q: Why does gonorrhoea treatment rely on a single high-dose parenteral cephalosporin today?
cards.a:
• N. gonorrhoeae has developed resistance to **penicillins, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones** and increasingly **azithromycin**; reduced cephalosporin susceptibility is emerging
• A single **IM ceftriaxone** dose gives reliable levels and adherence
• **Culture with sensitivity** and national surveillance (**NPHL sentinel surveillance**) track resistance
• Treatment failure must be cultured and reported

cards.q: Chlamydia: epidemiology, serovars and incubation?
cards.a:
• **Commonest bacterial STI**; highest prevalence in **under-25s**
• **Majority asymptomatic** in both sexes
• **C. trachomatis serovars D–K** (L1–L3 cause LGV)
• Incubation **7–21 days** (usually 5–15)
cards.m: D to K for the Kidding-age genitals; L for Lymph nodes (LGV).

cards.q: Clinical features of chlamydia in women and men?
cards.a:
• **Women**: mostly asymptomatic; mucopurulent discharge, **cervicitis**, dysuria, **intermenstrual/post-coital bleeding**, lower abdominal pain/PID
• **Men**: mucopurulent urethral discharge, dysuria, **epididymo-orchitis**
• Both: ano-rectal discomfort/discharge after receptive anal sex

cards.q: List the complications of chlamydia.
cards.a:
• **PID → ectopic pregnancy, infertility**
• **Sexually acquired reactive arthritis (SARA)**
• **Perihepatitis**, prostatitis
• Periurethral and perianal abscess
• Pregnancy: **PROM, preterm delivery, low birth weight**
• Neonate: ophthalmia neonatorum, pneumonia
cards.m: Silent infection, loud consequences – tubal infertility.

cards.q: What does a Gram stain show in chlamydial infection?
cards.a:
• Not diagnostic – no organisms seen
• **Increased polymorphs**: average **>5 per HPF in a urethral smear**, **>20 per HPF in an endocervical smear**
• Used to **exclude Gram-negative intracellular diplococci** (gonorrhoea)

cards.q: Which specimens are used for chlamydia NAAT, and what test should NOT be used?
cards.a:
• **Men**: first-pass urine
• **Women**: **self-collected vulvovaginal swab** (choice); endocervical swab if speculum done
• **Anorectal swab**: anyone with ano-rectal symptoms and **all MSM**
• **Pharyngeal swab**: all MSM
• **Chlamydia serology is not recommended** for diagnosis

cards.q: Treatment of uncomplicated chlamydia (urogenital, anorectal, pharyngeal)?
cards.a:
• **Doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 7 days** (preferred – better for rectal infection)
• Alternative: **azithromycin 1g PO STAT**
• Abstain from condomless sex until both partners have **completed the 7-day course** and symptoms resolve
cards.m: Doxy for a week beats azithro once – especially in the rectum.

cards.q: How is chlamydia treated in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Azithromycin 1g PO STAT** (preferred)
• Alternative: **amoxicillin 500mg PO q8h for 7 days**
• **Doxycycline is contraindicated** in pregnancy
• **Test of cure is recommended** in pregnancy (≥4 weeks after treatment)
cards.m: Pregnant? Swap the 'D' (doxy) for the 'A's (azithro, amoxicillin).

cards.q: When is a test of cure (TOC) for chlamydia recommended, and when should it be done?
cards.a:
• **Not routine** for uncomplicated genital chlamydia
• Recommended in **pregnancy**, **suspected poor compliance**, and **persistent symptoms**
• Do it **no earlier than 4 weeks after treatment** – residual non-viable DNA is detectable by NAAT for up to 4 weeks (false positive)
cards.m: Dead chlamydia DNA haunts the NAAT for a month.

cards.q: Partner management after a chlamydia diagnosis?
cards.a:
• Partners **within the last 60 days**: **treat epidemiologically regardless of test results**
• **Newborns of infected mothers must be screened**
• Abstain until both treated (7-day course completed) and symptoms resolved

cards.q: What are the causes of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU)?
cards.a:
• **Chlamydia trachomatis** (11–50%)
• **Mycoplasma genitalium** (6–50%)
• **Ureaplasma** spp. (11–26%)
• **Trichomonas vaginalis** (1–20%)
• **Adenovirus** (2–4%) and **HSV** (2–3%)
• Non-infectious causes also exist
cards.m: NGU = 'C-M-U-T-A-H': Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Ureaplasma, Trich, Adeno, Herpes.

cards.q: NGU: incubation and clinical features?
cards.a:
• Incubation variable, often longer than gonorrhoea: **1–3 weeks (up to 6)**
• Discharge **mucoid or mucopurulent**, may only appear on **urethral milking**
• Dysuria, urethral itch, penile irritation, frequency
• May be asymptomatic
• Associated: balanoposthitis, epididymo-orchitis, **SARA**

cards.q: How is NGU diagnosed?
cards.a:
• **Urethral Gram stain: ≥5 polymorphs per HPF** and **no Gram-negative intracellular diplococci**
• Urine FEME (leucocytes) and C&S to exclude UTI
• Urine **CT/NG NAAT**; urethral wet mount for T. vaginalis
• **Multiplex PCR** for recurrent/persistent NGU (M. genitalium)
• Little justification for urethral microscopy in **asymptomatic** men

cards.q: Treatment and partner advice for a first episode of NGU?
cards.a:
• **Doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 7 days**
• Alternative: **azithromycin 500mg STAT then 250mg daily for 4 days**
• Partners in the **preceding 60 days**: evaluate and give **chlamydia-active** treatment
• Abstain until treatment completed, partners treated and symptoms resolved for **1 week**
• Offer HIV and syphilis tests; **no TOC** if asymptomatic

cards.q: Treatment of recurrent or persistent NGU?
cards.a:
• Covers **M. genitalium** and **T. vaginalis**
• After **doxycycline** first line: **azithromycin 500mg STAT then 250mg daily for 4 days + metronidazole 400mg q12h 5 days**
• After **azithromycin** first line: **moxifloxacin 400mg daily 10–14 days + metronidazole 400mg q12h 5 days**
• Check adherence and re-exposure first
cards.m: Same logic as persistent urethral discharge: change class, add metronidazole.

cards.q: Define epididymo-orchitis and its usual route of infection.
cards.a:
• Syndrome of **pain, swelling and inflammation of the epididymis and/or testis**
• Usually **ascending, local extension from the urethra** (or bladder)

cards.q: How does the likely cause of epididymo-orchitis differ by age?
cards.a:
• **Under 35 years**: usually **sexually transmitted** – **C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae**
• **Over 35 years**: usually **enteric/urinary Gram-negatives** (e.g. **E. coli**)
• Older men often have **anatomical/functional urinary abnormalities** (e.g. BPH, instrumentation) – investigate further
• Risk history trumps age: an older man with STI risk can have an STI cause
cards.m: Under 35: Sex. Over 35: Sewage (E. coli).

cards.q: What must be excluded FIRST in a man with acute scrotal pain, and what else is on the differential?
cards.a:
• **Testicular torsion** – a **surgical emergency**; consider in all, exclude first (sudden severe pain, younger age, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex)
• Others: torsion of appendix testis, **testicular tumour**, hydrocoele, spermatocoele, varicocoele, trauma/rupture, **TB, mumps**
cards.m: Torsion first: the testis has about 6 hours.

cards.q: Clinical features of epididymo-orchitis?
cards.a:
• Usually **unilateral** testicular pain and swelling (onset over hours–days)
• **Palpable, tender swollen epididymis**
• Scrotal erythema/oedema
• **Urethritis symptoms or discharge**, dysuria
• Pyrexia

cards.q: Investigations for epididymo-orchitis?
cards.a:
• **Urethral Gram stain** – polymorphs, Gram-negative intracellular diplococci
• **Urethral swab for gonococcal culture**
• **Urine NAAT** for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis
• **Urine FEME and MSU culture** to exclude UTI
• **Surgical review / testicular ultrasound** if concerned (torsion, abscess, tumour)

cards.q: Treatment of STI-related epididymo-orchitis?
cards.a:
• **Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT PLUS doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 10 days**
• STI-related but **gonorrhoea unlikely** (e.g. Gram stain negative): **doxycycline 100mg q12h for 10–14 days**
• Plus **scrotal support** and **NSAIDs**
cards.m: Same two drugs as urethritis, but doxy runs 10 days not 7.

cards.q: Treatment of epididymo-orchitis due to enteric/urinary organisms?
cards.a:
• **Levofloxacin 500mg PO daily for 10 days**
• Alternative: **ofloxacin 200mg PO q12h for 14 days**
• Look for underlying urinary tract abnormality

cards.q: Follow-up of epididymo-orchitis: when to review and what to watch for?
cards.a:
• **No improvement after 3 days** → **review the diagnosis** (torsion, abscess, tumour)
• Review at **2 weeks**: compliance, partner notification, symptom resolution
• Abstain until patient and partner complete treatment; trace partners
• Complications: **hydrocoele, abscess, testicular infarction, infertility**

cards.q: Why do NSAIDs and scrotal support matter in epididymo-orchitis?
cards.a:
• **Scrotal support/elevation** reduces venous congestion and pain
• **NSAIDs** reduce inflammation and pain while antibiotics act
• Both are part of the guideline's general management alongside antibiotics

cards.q: Define ophthalmia neonatorum.
cards.a:
• **Conjunctivitis in the first 4 weeks of life**
• Eyelid and palpebral conjunctival **erythema and oedema**
• **Purulent eye discharge**
• **≥1 polymorph per oil-immersion field** on Gram-stained conjunctival smear

cards.q: What causes ophthalmia neonatorum, and which is commonest?
cards.a:
• **Chlamydia trachomatis – the commonest**
• **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** – the most destructive
• **HSV-1 and HSV-2**
• Others: Staph. aureus, Strep. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Pseudomonas, enteric Gram-negatives
cards.m: Chlamydia is Common; Gonorrhoea is Grave.

cards.q: Incubation periods of the causes of ophthalmia neonatorum?
cards.a:
• **Gonococcal: 2–5 days**
• **Chlamydial: 5–14 days**
• **Herpes simplex: 6–14 days**
cards.m: Gonococcus Goes first (2–5 days); Chlamydia Comes later (5–14).

cards.q: Why is ophthalmia neonatorum an emergency, and what are its complications?
cards.a:
• Watery exudate rapidly becomes **purulent, thick, blood-stained**; lids and conjunctiva oedematous
• Untreated: **keratitis, iridocyclitis, corneal ulceration and perforation**, pannus, scarring → **blindness** (especially gonococcal)
• Chlamydial infection may persist and cause **pharyngitis and pneumonia**

cards.q: What is special about herpes simplex neonatal conjunctivitis?
cards.a:
• Part of **generalised neonatal HSV** – skin, eye, mucosa
• Vesicles around the eye ± corneal involvement
• Needs a **lumbar puncture** and **ophthalmology assessment**
• Treat with **IV acyclovir 10mg/kg/dose q8h for 2 weeks** (per ON table)

cards.q: Investigations for ophthalmia neonatorum?
cards.a:
• **Eye swab Gram stain** – fresh, reaching the lab **within 30 minutes**
• Gram-negative intracellular diplococci: high sensitivity and specificity for gonorrhoea
• Eye swab **culture and sensitivity**
• **NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis**; swab for **HSV NAAT**
• Check **RPR of infant and mother**; screen for HIV

cards.q: Treatment of gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum?
cards.a:
• **Systemic: ceftriaxone 25–50mg/kg (max 250mg) IV/IM STAT** (alternative cefotaxime 100mg/kg STAT)
• **Local**: irrigate with sterile saline **at least hourly** until discharge clears; topical antibiotics optional
• Disseminated: ceftriaxone daily for **7 days** (meningitis 10–14 days)
• Refer to **ophthalmologist**
cards.m: Gonococcal eyes: one systemic jab + hourly washes.

cards.q: Treatment of chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum, and its key adverse effect?
cards.a:
• **Systemic treatment is essential** (topical alone does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage or prevent pneumonia)
• **Erythromycin 50mg/kg/day PO in 4 divided doses for 14 days**
• Alternative: **azithromycin 20mg/kg PO daily for 3 days**
• May need a repeat course (cure 80–100%)
• Both linked to **infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis**
cards.m: Chlamydia lives in the nose and lungs too – drops are not enough.

cards.q: What else must be done for the family of a baby with ophthalmia neonatorum?
cards.a:
• **Refer parents to an STI clinic** – screen especially for C. trachomatis, HSV and HIV
• **Treat the mother epidemiologically**
• Check **RPR in mother and infant** (associated congenital syphilis)
• Careful handling to prevent spread; notify as required

cards.q: Follow-up after treatment of ophthalmia neonatorum?
cards.a:
• Review **2 weeks after discharge**
• **Repeat eye swab Gram stain and culture**
• Persistent signs → consider a **second course** of treatment

cards.q: Define pelvic inflammatory disease.
cards.a:
• Spectrum of inflammation of the **upper female genital tract**
• Usually **ascending infection from the endocervix**
• Includes **endometritis, salpingitis, parametritis, oophoritis, tubo-ovarian abscess, pelvic peritonitis**

cards.q: What organisms cause PID?
cards.a:
• Often **polymicrobial**
• STI: **N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis** (younger women); **M. genitalium**
• Non-STI: **anaerobes**, Gardnerella, H. influenzae, enteric Gram-negatives, Strep. agalactiae, CMV, M. hominis, Ureaplasma
• **Pathogen-negative** PID is common (false-positive diagnosis, other cause, or cervical infection already cleared)
cards.m: That is why PID needs three drugs: ceftriaxone (GC), doxy (CT), metronidazole (anaerobes).

cards.q: Symptoms and signs of PID?
cards.a:
• **Bilateral lower abdominal pain** (typical)
• **Deep dyspareunia**
• Abnormal bleeding: post-coital, intermenstrual, menorrhagia
• Purulent vaginal/cervical discharge
• Fever **>38°C**
• **Adnexal tenderness** and **cervical motion tenderness** on bimanual examination

cards.q: Why must PID be diagnosed with caution, and what must be excluded?
cards.a:
• Symptoms and signs have **low sensitivity and specificity**
• Diagnosis on examination findings **without lower abdominal pain** should be made with caution
• Exclude **ectopic pregnancy**, endometriosis, **ovarian cyst complications**, **acute appendicitis**, UTI

cards.q: What is the value of the vaginal smear pus-cell count in suspected PID?
cards.a:
• **Absence** of endocervical/vaginal pus cells has a good **negative predictive value (95%)** – PID unlikely
• **Presence** is non-specific: **positive predictive value only 17%**
cards.m: No pus, probably no PID; pus proves nothing.

cards.q: Which investigations are recommended in suspected PID?
cards.a:
• **Pregnancy test** in all women of reproductive age (exclude ectopic)
• **Endocervical swabs**: gonococcal microscopy/culture and **chlamydia NAAT**
• **Screen for STIs including HIV**
• **Ultrasound** of limited value in uncomplicated PID – useful if **abscess or hydrosalpinx** suspected
• MRI/CT not routine

cards.q: Why is PID treated empirically as soon as it is suspected?
cards.a:
• No definitive clinical diagnostic criteria
• **Delay increases long-term sequelae**: **ectopic pregnancy, infertility, chronic pelvic pain**
• So a **low threshold** for empirical treatment
cards.m: When in doubt about PID, treat – the tubes cannot wait for swabs.

cards.q: When should a woman with PID be admitted (preferably under gynaecology)?
cards.a:
• **Surgical emergency cannot be excluded** (e.g. appendicitis, ectopic)
• **Lack of response or intolerance to oral therapy**
• **Clinically severe** disease – **fever >38°C, signs of peritonitis**
• **Tubo-ovarian abscess**
• **PID in pregnancy**
cards.m: Admit if 'SOS-TP': Surgical doubt, Oral failure, Severe, Tubo-ovarian abscess, Pregnant.

cards.q: Outpatient treatment of mild–moderate PID?
cards.a:
• **Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT**
• **PLUS doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 14 days**
• **PLUS metronidazole 400mg PO q12h for 14 days**
• Alternative: ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT + **azithromycin 1g weekly for 2 weeks** + metronidazole 14 days
• Provide analgesia
cards.m: PID = 1 jab + 2 tablets for 2 weeks.

cards.q: Can IM ceftriaxone be replaced by oral cefixime in PID? What if the patient is cephalosporin-allergic?
cards.a:
• **No** – no trial evidence for oral cephalosporins and tissue levels are likely lower
• Cephalosporin allergy **and low gonorrhoea risk**: **levofloxacin 500mg daily 14 days + metronidazole 400mg q12h 14 days**, OR **moxifloxacin 400mg daily 14 days** alone

cards.q: Inpatient regimen for severe PID?
cards.a:
• **Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily + doxycycline 100mg PO q12h + metronidazole** (400mg PO or 500mg IV q12h)
• Alternatives: clindamycin 900mg IV q8h + gentamicin; or ampicillin/sulbactam 3g IV q6h + doxycycline
• **Switch to oral after 24–48 hours of clinical improvement**; total **14 days**

cards.q: How is PID managed in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• Uncommon but raises **maternal and foetal morbidity** → **admit, parenteral therapy**
• No regimen of proven safety; cover gonorrhoea, chlamydia and anaerobes – e.g. **parenteral ceftriaxone + erythromycin + metronidazole**, oral after response, total 2 weeks
• **Avoid doxycycline**

cards.q: Should an IUD be removed in a woman with PID?
cards.a:
• **Not automatically** – balance against **pregnancy risk if she had unprotected sex in the preceding 7 days**
• **Consider removal if no response within 48–72 hours**
• Hormonal **emergency contraception** may be appropriate if removed
• PID risk from insertion is increased only in the **first 3 weeks** and is **<1%**
cards.m: Treat the woman first, the device later.

cards.q: Partner management and follow-up in PID?
cards.a:
• Partners **within 60 days**: treat epidemiologically for **chlamydia and gonorrhoea** regardless of tests
• Avoid intercourse until both complete treatment
• **Review at 72 hours** – no improvement → further investigation, **parenteral therapy** and/or surgery
• **Review again at 2–4 weeks**: response, compliance, contact tracing, counselling on sequelae
• Highest-risk group: **under 25**, new partner, no barrier contraception
cards.m: PID reviews: 3 days, then 2–4 weeks.

cards.q: What is the role of surgery in PID?
cards.a:
• **Laparoscopy** can divide adhesions and drain pelvic abscesses
• **Ultrasound-guided aspiration** of collections is less invasive and may be equally effective
• **Laparotomy** for clinically severe pelvic infection

cards.q: Trichomonas vaginalis: what is it and how is it transmitted?
cards.a:
• **Flagellated protozoan** parasite of the genital tract; thrives at **pH 4.9–7.5**
• **Almost exclusively sexually transmitted** (intravaginal/intraurethral inoculation)
• Found in 14–60% of male partners of infected women and 67–100% of female partners of infected men
• Incubation **4 days – 4 weeks**
cards.m: Trich is a true STI – unlike BV and thrush.

cards.q: Clinical features of trichomoniasis in women?
cards.a:
• 10–50% asymptomatic
• **Vaginal discharge** – classically **frothy yellow(-green)**, offensive; thin to thick
• **Vulval itching**, dysuria, offensive odour
• **Strawberry cervix** (punctate haemorrhages) – only **~2% visible to the naked eye**, more on colposcopy
• Sometimes lower abdominal discomfort, post-coital bleeding
cards.m: Frothy, fishy, itchy, and a strawberry you rarely see.

cards.q: How does trichomoniasis present in men?
cards.a:
• **15–50% asymptomatic**; often present as **partners of infected women**
• Urethral discharge and/or dysuria, urethral irritation, frequency
• Examination often **normal**; discharge in 20–60%
• Rarely balanoposthitis, penile ulceration
• A cause of **persistent NGU**

cards.q: How is trichomoniasis diagnosed?
cards.a:
• **Saline wet mount** – **motile trichomonads**; sample from **posterior fornix**; sensitivity only **40–60%**
• Examine **immediately** – motility fades with time
• **NAAT** if available – sensitivity **88–100%**, specificity 92–100%
cards.m: Wet mount: look fast, they stop swimming.

cards.q: Treatment of trichomoniasis?
cards.a:
• **Metronidazole 400mg PO q12h for 7 days** (preferred)
• OR **metronidazole 2g PO STAT** – more GI upset and **higher failure**, especially if partners not treated together
• Spontaneous cure only 20–25% – treat to eradicate urethral/paraurethral gland infection
• Advise **no alcohol** during and for 48h after metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction)

cards.q: Trichomoniasis in pregnancy: risks and treatment?
cards.a:
• Associated with **preterm delivery and low birth weight**
• **Routine screening** of asymptomatic pregnant women **not recommended**
• **Metronidazole is safe in all trimesters** and breastfeeding (no teratogenicity in 1st trimester)
• Use the **7-day regimen** – **single high-dose (2g) regimens are not recommended** in pregnancy

cards.q: Partner management and test of cure in trichomoniasis?
cards.a:
• **Treat sexual partners simultaneously**
• Avoid sex (including oral) for **at least 1 week** and until both complete treatment
• **TOC (NAAT)** only if symptoms **persist or recur** – including pregnant women
cards.m: Trich ping-pongs between partners unless both are treated at once.

cards.q: What causes vulvovaginal candidiasis, and is it an STI?
cards.a:
• **Candida albicans ~90%**, C. glabrata ~8%, others (C. tropicalis, krusei, parapsilosis)
• **Not sexually transmitted** – overgrowth of commensal yeast
• **Contact tracing not required**; no evidence for treating asymptomatic male partners
cards.m: Thrush is a guest that overstays, not one brought by a partner.

cards.q: Symptoms and signs of vulvovaginal candidiasis?
cards.a:
• **Vulval itch/burning**, soreness, superficial dyspareunia, dysuria
• Discharge **thick, white, curdy** (cottage-cheese) – may be normal or absent
• **Erythematous, excoriated, swollen vulva**; satellite pustulopapular lesions
• Vaginal wall erythema with adherent white discharge; **cervix normal**
• Vaginal pH normal (≤4.5)

cards.q: Define recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis and list predisposing factors.
cards.a:
• **≥4 episodes in 12 months** (nearly 10% of women)
• Confirm by **culture at least once**
• Predisposing: **diabetes**, **HIV**/immunosuppression, **corticosteroids**, frequent **broad-spectrum antibiotics**, poor adherence to antifungals
cards.m: Four a year = recurrent: check sugar, HIV and steroids.

cards.q: How is vulvovaginal candidiasis confirmed in the lab?
cards.a:
• **Gram stain** of discharge: **blastospores and pseudohyphae** (guideline text misprints 'blastopores')
• **10% KOH** preparation shows yeast/hyphae
• **Culture** for symptomatic women with **negative microscopy**, and for recurrent cases (species, e.g. C. glabrata)

cards.q: Treatment regimens for uncomplicated, severe and recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis?
cards.a:
• **Uncomplicated**: **clotrimazole 500mg pessary STAT** or **fluconazole 150–200mg PO STAT** (similar efficacy)
• **Complicated/severe**: **fluconazole 150–200mg every 72h for 2–3 doses**
• **Recurrent**: **fluconazole 150–200mg q72h x3 (induction), then weekly for 6 months** (or clotrimazole 500mg pessary weekly 6 months)
• Treat vulva and vagina; 1% hydrocortisone for itch; avoid soaps/douches
cards.m: Recurrent thrush: 3 to knock it down, weekly for 6 months to keep it down.

cards.q: How is vulvovaginal candidiasis treated in pregnancy, and why?
cards.a:
• **Topical azoles only** – e.g. **clotrimazole vaginal pessary**
• **Oral fluconazole/azoles avoided** (conflicting safety evidence)
• Pregnant women may need a **longer topical course (minimum 7 days)**
• Antifungal creams can **damage latex condoms**

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of bacterial vaginosis?
cards.a:
• Normal **lactobacilli** make **lactic acid** (pH 3.5–4.5), hydrogen peroxide and bacteriocins, and block adhesion sites
• In BV, lactobacilli are **replaced by an overgrowth of anaerobes** (BV-associated bacteria: **Gardnerella vaginalis**, Mobiluncus, Bacteroides)
• **pH rises above 4.5**; amines produce the fishy odour
• **Commonest cause of vaginal discharge** in reproductive-age women
cards.m: BV = lost lactobacilli, not a new invader.

cards.q: What are the associations and triggers of bacterial vaginosis?
cards.a:
• Associations: **new or more lifetime partners**, **smoking**, **IUD**, co-existing STI/PID
• Triggers: **unprotected sex** (alkaline semen), **menstruation**, **vaginal douching**
• Less common with hormonal contraception and condoms
• Does not occur in **prepubertal girls**; uncommon after menopause; **men do not get BV**

cards.q: Clinical presentation of bacterial vaginosis?
cards.a:
• **Thin, watery, homogeneous** white/grey discharge coating the vaginal walls
• **Offensive fishy odour** (~50%), often worse after sex or menses
• **~50% asymptomatic**
• **No inflammation** – vulval soreness in <10% (suggests another cause)
• Differentials: trichomoniasis, candidiasis, cervicitis
cards.m: BV smells but does not sting; thrush stings but does not smell.

cards.q: What are Amsel's criteria for bacterial vaginosis?
cards.a:
Diagnosis needs **at least 3 of 4**:
• **Thin, white, homogeneous discharge**
• **Clue cells** on wet mount
• Vaginal **pH >4.5**
• **Fishy odour on adding 10% KOH** (whiff test)
cards.m: Amsel's 'DCPW': Discharge, Clue cells, pH, Whiff – 3 of 4.

cards.q: What are the Hay/Ison criteria for Gram-stained vaginal smears?
cards.a:
• **Grade 1 (normal)**: lactobacilli predominate
• **Grade 2 (intermediate)**: mixed flora – some lactobacilli plus Gardnerella/Mobiluncus
• **Grade 3 (BV)**: predominantly Gardnerella/Mobiluncus, **few or absent lactobacilli**
• Grade 4: Gram-positive cocci predominate
• (The **Nugent score** is the research equivalent: 7–10 = BV)

cards.q: Treatment of bacterial vaginosis?
cards.a:
• Treat **symptomatic** women
• **Metronidazole 400mg PO q12h for 5–7 days** (best cure rates)
• Alternatives: **clindamycin 300mg PO q12h for 7 days**, or **metronidazole 2g PO STAT** (more GI upset)
• Relapse common: ~30% at 1 month, up to 60% at 6 months
• Avoid douching, shower gel and antiseptic soaps

cards.q: Bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy and partner management?
cards.a:
• BV raises risk of **second-trimester miscarriage (3–5-fold)** and **preterm birth**
• **Treat symptomatic** pregnant women (oral or vaginal); screening may benefit those at **high risk of preterm birth**
• **Metronidazole is not teratogenic** (1st trimester data reassuring) and is acceptable in breastfeeding
• **Male partners: no routine screening or treatment**; no test of cure
cards.m: BV is not an STI to treat in the partner.

cards.q: How do the discharges of bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis and candidiasis differ at the bedside?
cards.a:
• **BV**: thin, grey-white, homogeneous, **fishy**; no inflammation; **pH >4.5**; clue cells
• **Trichomoniasis**: **frothy yellow-green**, offensive; vulvitis, **strawberry cervix**; **pH raised (organism thrives at 4.9–7.5)**; motile trichomonads
• **Candidiasis**: **thick white curdy**, little odour; **itchy red swollen vulva**; **pH normal (≤4.5)**; pseudohyphae
• Cervical **mucopurulent** discharge points instead to gonorrhoea/chlamydia
cards.m: Fishy = BV, Frothy = Trich, Floury/curdy = Candida.

cards.q: HSV-1 vs HSV-2 in genital herpes?
cards.a:
• **HSV-1**: usual cause of oro-labial herpes and **now the commonest cause of genital herpes** (>50% of primary genital infections in young people)
• **HSV-2**: historically commonest; **recurs far more often** (median **0.34 vs 0.08** recurrences/month)
• Incubation **2–14 days**
cards.m: HSV-1 is now the commonest first episode; HSV-2 is the one that keeps coming back.

cards.q: Define primary, non-primary first episode and recurrent genital herpes.
cards.a:
• **Primary**: first infection with HSV-1 or 2 in someone with **no antibodies to either type** – most severe, heals within ~a month
• **Non-primary**: first symptoms with one type in someone **with antibodies to the other** – milder, heals in 1–2 weeks
• **Recurrent**: **reactivation** of latent virus from sensory ganglia – milder, unilateral, heals in 1–2 weeks

cards.q: What is asymptomatic viral shedding and why does it matter?
cards.a:
• **80%** of infected people have no symptoms
• Virus shed from **intact skin without lesions**
• Accounts for **~70% of transmission**
• Most common with **HSV-2**, in the **first year**, and with **frequent recurrences**
• So **consistent condom use** is advised; transmission may come from a partner infected years earlier
cards.m: Most herpes is passed on by people who don't know they are shedding.

cards.q: Clinical features of a first episode vs a recurrence of genital herpes?
cards.a:
• **First episode**: **painful bilateral** blisters/ulcers, **tender bilateral inguinal nodes**, dysuria, discharge, **fever and myalgia** (systemic symptoms mainly in primary)
• **Recurrence**: **unilateral**, limited to one dermatome, milder, often preceded by **prodrome** (tingling)
• Triggers: trauma, **menstruation**, fever, immunosuppression, stress, **UV light**

cards.q: What are the complications of genital herpes?
cards.a:
• **Secondary infection** with Candida or streptococci (usually 2nd week)
• **Autonomic neuropathy → urinary retention**
• **Aseptic meningitis**
• Severe: disseminated infection, pneumonitis, hepatitis, encephalitis

cards.q: Best laboratory test for genital herpes, and which tests to avoid?
cards.a:
• **HSV NAAT/PCR** of vesicle fluid or lesion swab – **sensitivity and specificity >90%**, gives type, useful at all stages
• Viral culture: specific but **low sensitivity**
• **Type-specific serology**: takes 8–12 weeks; **not routine in asymptomatic** people (poor predictive value)
• **Tzanck smear** (multinucleated giant cells): **insensitive and non-specific – do not rely on it**
cards.m: Swab the sore for PCR; skip the Tzanck.

cards.q: Treatment of a first episode of genital herpes?
cards.a:
• Start **on clinical suspicion**, without waiting for tests
• Give if presenting **within 5 days** of onset or while **new lesions are still forming**
• **Acyclovir 400mg PO q8h for 7–10 days** (or valacyclovir 1g q12h 7–10 days)
• **Topical antivirals not recommended**
• Antivirals do **not alter the natural history** (latency persists)
cards.m: First episode: 400 three times a day for 7–10 days.

cards.q: Supportive care and complication management in first-episode herpes?
cards.a:
• **Saline or dilute potassium permanganate** sitz baths
• Analgesia, **topical lidocaine**
• Women with severe dysuria: **pass urine in a warm bath**
• Admit for **urinary retention, meningism**, severe systemic illness
• If catheter needed, consider **suprapubic** route (less ascending infection and pain; allows trial of voiding)

cards.q: Episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes: who and how?
cards.a:
• For patients with **severe or prominent prodromal** recurrences
• **Patient-initiated within 24 hours** of symptoms – can abort lesions in up to one-third
• **Acyclovir 800mg PO q8h for 2 days** OR **800mg q12h for 5 days**
• (Valacyclovir 500mg q12h 3 days or 1g daily 5 days)
• Shortens episodes by a median of only **1–2 days**
cards.m: Episodic = pills in the pocket, take at the first tingle.

cards.q: Suppressive antiviral therapy for genital herpes: indication and regimen?
cards.a:
• **≥6 recurrences per year**, or severe/prolonged episodes, or psychosocial distress
• **Acyclovir 400mg PO q12h** for up to **1 year, then reassess**
• Breakthrough recurrences → increase to 400mg q8h
• Reduces recurrences by **70–80%** but **does not eliminate subclinical shedding**
• Full effect after about **5 days**
cards.m: Six or more a year → suppress.

cards.q: First episode genital herpes in the 1st or 2nd trimester (up to 27+6 weeks): management?
cards.a:
• **Oral acyclovir 400mg TDS for 7–10 days** (IV if disseminated)
• Acyclovir is considered **safe** (not linked to birth defects)
• Paracetamol, topical lidocaine 2%; **inform the obstetrician**
• If delivery is not within 6 weeks → **expectant management and vaginal delivery anticipated**

cards.q: First episode genital herpes in the 3rd trimester (from 28 weeks): management?
cards.a:
• Treat without delay: **acyclovir 400mg TDS continued until delivery**
• **Caesarean section recommended** – especially if symptoms arise **within 6 weeks of delivery**
• Neonatal transmission risk with vaginal delivery is **~41%** (no protective maternal antibodies yet)
• Treat **all first-episode lesions as primary** (up to 15% are actually recurrences)
cards.m: Primary herpes near term = 41% risk = caesarean.

cards.q: Recurrent genital herpes in pregnancy: delivery and treatment?
cards.a:
• Neonatal herpes risk is **low (0–3%)** even with lesions at delivery – **maternal IgG protects the baby**
• **Vaginal delivery** should be offered
• Consider **suppressive acyclovir 400mg TDS from 36 weeks** to reduce lesions and caesareans
• Baby: conservative management, no swabs or treatment needed
cards.m: Recurrent herpes at term: 0–3% risk – deliver vaginally.

cards.q: A well baby is born vaginally to a mother with primary HSV within the last 6 weeks. What is done?
cards.a:
• **Swabs** (skin, conjunctiva, oropharynx, rectum) for **HSV PCR**
• **Lumbar puncture not necessary** if the baby is well
• **Empirical IV acyclovir 20mg/kg q8h** until infection is excluded
• Strict infection control; **breastfeeding encouraged** unless nipple lesions
• Unwell baby or lesions → also **LP**; neonatal herpes treated 14 days (skin) or 21 days (CNS/disseminated)

cards.q: What should be covered when counselling a patient newly diagnosed with genital herpes?
cards.a:
• Natural course: **latency and recurrences**, recurrences become less frequent over time
• **Subclinical shedding** – transmission possible without lesions
• **Treatment options** (episodic vs suppressive)
• **Abstain during lesions and prodrome**; **consistent condom use** otherwise
• Risk to the baby at birth (if pregnant or planning)
• Partner notification – infection may have come from an **asymptomatic partner years earlier** (not proof of infidelity)

cards.q: Which HPV types cause genital warts, and which cause cancer?
cards.a:
• **Low-risk HPV 6 and 11** → **genital warts** and **recurrent respiratory papillomatosis**
• **High-risk (oncogenic) HPV 16, 18**, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 → cervical, penile, vulval, vaginal, anal and oropharyngeal cancers
• HPV: non-enveloped dsDNA virus; ~40 types infect the genital area
cards.m: 6 and 11 make warts; 16 and 18 make cancer.

cards.q: How is genital HPV transmitted?
cards.a:
• **Highly contagious** – **>75% of partners** develop warts after exposure
• **Penetrative and non-penetrative** sexual contact (vaginal, anal, oral)
• Risk rises with **number of partners**
• **Perinatal** (rare) – HPV 6/11 respiratory papillomatosis
• Digital spread in children; fomites – no good evidence

cards.q: Clinical types and common sites of anogenital warts?
cards.a:
• Types: **condylomata acuminata**, flat papules/plaques, keratotic (verruca vulgaris-type), **giant condyloma (Buschke-Löwenstein)**, laryngeal papilloma
• Sites: vaginal introitus, **foreskin** (uncircumcised), **shaft** (circumcised), cervix, urethra, perianal/anal
• **Intra-anal warts** suggest **receptive anal sex**
• Mostly asymptomatic; itch, bleeding, psychological distress

cards.q: How are genital warts diagnosed, and when is a biopsy needed?
cards.a:
• Usually by **visual inspection**
• **Biopsy** if **atypical**, diagnostic doubt, **not responding** to treatment, to **exclude malignancy**, and **all suspected cervical lesions**
• **HPV testing is not recommended** for warts – does not confirm or guide management
• Cervical cytology as per screening

cards.q: Patient-applied treatments for external anogenital warts?
cards.a:
• **Imiquimod 5% cream 3 times/week at bedtime**, up to 16 weeks (immune modifier)
• **Podofilox (podophyllotoxin) 0.5%** twice daily for **3 days, then 4 days off**, up to 4 cycles
• Sinecatechins 15% ointment
• Imiquimod and podofilox **may weaken condoms and diaphragms**
cards.m: Podophyllotoxin: 3 on, 4 off.

cards.q: Provider-administered treatments for genital warts, and a key safety caution?
cards.a:
• **Cryotherapy** with liquid nitrogen or cryoprobe
• **Surgical removal** – scissor/shave excision, curettage, laser, electrosurgery
• **Trichloroacetic acid (TCA)** or bichloroacetic acid applied weekly
• Meatal, vaginal, cervical, intra-anal warts: cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen), surgery or TCA
• **No cryoprobe in the vagina** – risk of **perforation and fistula**
• Cervical warts → specialist + **biopsy to exclude HSIL**; intra-anal → colorectal specialist

cards.q: How are genital warts managed in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Podofilox/podophyllin and sinecatechins must not be used** (teratogenic/toxic)
• **Imiquimod avoided** until more data
• Use **cryotherapy, TCA or surgical removal**
• Warts may **proliferate and become friable**; may resolve poorly until after delivery
cards.m: Podophyllin in pregnancy = poison.

cards.q: Is caesarean section indicated for genital warts in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Not to prevent HPV transmission** – unclear whether CS prevents respiratory papillomatosis
• **CS indicated only** if warts **obstruct the pelvic outlet** or vaginal delivery would cause **excessive bleeding**
• Counsel about the **low risk of laryngeal papillomatosis** in the infant

cards.q: Follow-up and contact tracing for genital warts?
cards.a:
• Warts typically respond **within 3 months** of therapy
• Poor response: **immunosuppression**, poor compliance → reconsider/biopsy
• **Current partner** may benefit from examination and STI tests; inform current partners
• **Tracing previous partners is not recommended**
• Treatment does **not eradicate HPV** or reduce cancer risk

cards.q: Prevention advice for HPV and genital warts?
cards.a:
• **HPV vaccine** for males and females – can be given **regardless of past warts, abnormal smear or HPV result**
• **Consistent condom use** lowers (not abolishes) risk
• **Regular cervical screening (pap smear every 3 years)** for women with warts and those vaccinated
• Abstinence is the most reliable method
cards.m: Vaccine prevents, condoms reduce, screening detects.

cards.q: Chancroid: organism, incubation and ulcer characteristics?
cards.a:
• **Haemophilus ducreyi** (Gram-negative coccobacillus)
• Incubation **3–10 days**
• Papule → pustule → **multiple, painful, soft (non-indurated) ulcers**
• **Necrotic base, purulent exudate, ragged undermined edges**, **bleed easily**
• **'Kissing ulcers'** from autoinoculation
cards.m: Chancroid = 'soft chancre that makes you cry'; syphilis = 'hard chancre, no pain'.
