cards.q: What is the bubo of chancroid, and when can chancroid be diagnosed as 'probable'?
cards.a:
• **Painful, unilateral inguinal adenitis** in ~50% → **fluctuant buboes** that may rupture
• Probable chancroid requires **all**: one or more painful ulcers; **no T. pallidum** (syphilis serology done **≥7–14 days** after ulcer onset); typical clinical picture; **HSV PCR negative**

cards.q: Investigations for chancroid?
cards.a:
• **Gram stain** of ulcer base or bubo pus: Gram-negative coccobacilli in a **'school of fish'** pattern
• **Culture**: swab base and undermined edges after saline cleansing; plate at bedside or send in **Amies medium within 4 hours**
• **Multiplex PCR** (H. ducreyi, T. pallidum, HSV) – sensitivity >95%
• Always test for **syphilis and HSV** (co-infection, look-alikes) and HIV

cards.q: Treatment, bubo management and contact tracing in chancroid?
cards.a:
• **Azithromycin 1g PO STAT** (preferred; also in pregnancy)
• Alternatives: **ceftriaxone 250mg IM STAT**, ciprofloxacin 500mg q12h 3 days (not in pregnancy), erythromycin 800mg q8h 7 days
• Fluctuant buboes: **needle aspiration through adjacent healthy skin** (I&D risks sinus)
• Treat sex contacts from the **10 days before symptom onset**, even if asymptomatic
• Re-examine **3–7 days**; poorer response if **uncircumcised or HIV-positive**
cards.m: Chancroid look-back is only 10 days – the incubation is short.

cards.q: Lymphogranuloma venereum: organism and why it behaves differently from ordinary chlamydia?
cards.a:
• **C. trachomatis serovars L1–L3** (**L2b** in MSM outbreaks; often HIV co-infection)
• Serovars A–K stay in the **mucosa**; L strains are **invasive** – spread through connective tissue to **regional lymph nodes**
• Incubation **3–30 days**

cards.q: Describe the three stages of LGV.
cards.a:
• **Primary**: small **painless papule/herpetiform ulcer** that **heals within a week** (often unnoticed); discharge or **proctitis**
• **Secondary** (2–6 weeks): **painful, usually unilateral inguino-femoral lymphadenopathy** → buboes (rupture in a third); **'groove sign'** (nodes above and below the inguinal ligament) in 15–20%; fever, systemic spread
• **Tertiary** ('anogenitorectal syndrome', mostly women): strictures, fistulae, **elephantiasis/'saxophone penis'**, **esthiomene**
cards.m: LGV: little painless sore, then big painful nodes with a groove, then scarring.

cards.q: How does LGV present in MSM?
cards.a:
• **Proctitis** is the main presentation
• **Haemopurulent discharge, severe anorectal pain, tenesmus**, rectal bleeding, constipation
• Anoscopy: haemorrhagic, ulcerative proctitis ± mass
• **Usually no inguinal lymphadenopathy**; 25% asymptomatic
• **Mimics Crohn's disease** clinically and histologically
cards.m: Young MSM with 'Crohn's proctitis' – test for LGV.

cards.q: Diagnosis and treatment of LGV?
cards.a:
• **Chlamydia NAAT** positive sample sent for **LGV-specific genotyping**
• **Doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 21 days**
• Alternatives: **azithromycin 1g weekly for 3 weeks** (pregnancy) or erythromycin 800mg q6h 21 days
• Buboes: **needle aspiration through healthy skin** – **incision not recommended** (sinus)
• Partners within **60 days**: asymptomatic → doxycycline 100mg BD **7 days**
• **Retest for chlamydia at ~3 months**
cards.m: LGV = 3 weeks of doxy (vs 1 week for ordinary chlamydia).

cards.q: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale): organism and clinical picture?
cards.a:
• **Klebsiella granulomatis** (formerly Calymmatobacterium)
• Incubation **2–4 weeks** (up to 50 days)
• **Painless**, slowly progressive nodules → **beefy-red, friable ulcers that bleed readily on touch**
• Types: ulcerogranulomatous, hypertrophic/verrucous, necrotic, sclerotic
• **Usually no lymphadenopathy** – **pseudobuboes** (subcutaneous granulomas)
cards.m: Donovanosis: beefy, bleeding, painless – and no real bubo.

cards.q: How is donovanosis confirmed?
cards.a:
• **Tissue smear/biopsy** stained with **Wright or Giemsa**: **Donovan bodies** (intracytoplasmic bacteria in macrophages), plasma cells and polymorphs
• **Molecular test** for K. granulomatis DNA

cards.q: Treatment and follow-up of donovanosis?
cards.a:
• **Azithromycin 1g PO weekly or 500mg daily** for **at least 3 weeks and until all lesions have healed**
• Alternatives: doxycycline 100mg q12h, co-trimoxazole 160/800mg q12h, erythromycin 800mg q6h (same duration)
• Pregnancy/lactation: **macrolide**; doxycycline contraindicated
• Partners within **60 days** screened and offered treatment
• Follow up **at least 1 year** – **relapse 6–18 months** later; risk of **SCC**
cards.m: Treat until healed, then watch for a year.

cards.q: Compare the genital ulcers of syphilis, herpes, chancroid, LGV and donovanosis by pain and nodes.
cards.a:
• **Primary syphilis**: single **painless, indurated** ulcer; **painless rubbery** nodes
• **Herpes**: **multiple painful vesicles/shallow ulcers**; tender bilateral nodes
• **Chancroid**: **painful soft ragged** ulcers; **painful suppurative bubo**
• **LGV**: **transient painless** ulcer; later **painful nodes, groove sign**
• **Donovanosis**: **painless beefy-red bleeding** ulcer; **no true nodes** (pseudobuboes)
cards.m: Painful ulcer: Herpes, cHancroid (the 'H's). Painless: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan 3 weeks after condomless vaginal sex with a casual female partner. He is asymptomatic and examination is normal. He requests STI screening today and asks which results he can rely on.
Which of the following tests, if negative today, reliably excludes infection acquired from that exposure?
o: HIV antigen/antibody combination test on blood
Syphilis serology (RPR plus TPPA) on blood
Chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT on first-pass urine
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) on venous blood
Hepatitis C antibody (anti-HCV) test
mcq.e: Window periods in the guideline: chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT 2 weeks, HIV Ag/Ab 4 weeks, syphilis serology 6–12 weeks, hepatitis B 3–6 months and hepatitis C up to 6 months. At 3 weeks only the CT/NG NAAT is outside its window, so the other tests must be repeated after their window periods. A known contact still inside a window period should be considered for treatment.
w: Wrong - The HIV Ag/Ab window period is 4 weeks; a negative result at 3 weeks must be repeated.
Wrong - Syphilis serology has a 6–12 week window; repeat later (or treat if a known contact).
Correct - The CT/NG NAAT window period is 2 weeks, so a negative result at 3 weeks is reliable.
Wrong - Hepatitis B has a window of 3–6 months; one negative HBsAg at 3 weeks is not reassuring.
Wrong - Hepatitis C antibodies may take up to 6 months to appear.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan for STI screening because her boyfriend has new dysuria. She has vaginal sex only, is asymptomatic and prefers not to have a speculum examination today.
Which is the specimen of choice for her chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT?
o: Self-collected vulvovaginal swab
First-pass urine sample
High vaginal swab sent for routine culture
Serum sample for chlamydia antibody serology
Urethral swab taken by the clinician
mcq.e: In women the self-collected vulvovaginal swab is the NAAT specimen of choice; an endocervical swab is used if a speculum examination is being done anyway. First-pass urine is the preferred specimen in men and only a fallback in women. Chlamydia serology is not recommended for diagnosis.
w: Correct - Self-collected vulvovaginal swabs are the preferred NAAT specimen in women and need no speculum.
Wrong - First-pass urine is preferred in men; in women it is only considered if vaginal or endocervical swabs cannot be taken.
Wrong - Routine HVS culture does not detect chlamydia and is less sensitive than NAAT for gonorrhoea.
Wrong - Chlamydia serology is not recommended for diagnosing current infection.
Wrong - Urethral swabs are less acceptable and are not the preferred female NAAT specimen.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man who has sex with men attends for routine screening. He reports receptive and insertive anal sex and receptive oral sex with several casual partners in the last 3 months, with inconsistent condom use. He is asymptomatic.
Which screening package is most appropriate?
o: Blood for HIV and syphilis serology plus first-pass urine CT/NG NAAT
Blood for HIV, syphilis, HBsAg and anti-HCV serology plus first-pass urine NAAT only
First-pass urine plus rectal and pharyngeal CT/NG NAAT, no blood tests
Blood for HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, anti-HCV; urine, rectal and pharyngeal NAAT
Blood for HIV and syphilis serology plus a urethral Gram stain only
mcq.e: MSM should have blood for HIV Ag/Ab and syphilis serology, and unprotected sex with MSM is a blood-borne virus risk, so HBsAg and anti-HCV are added. CT/NG NAAT on first-pass urine plus pharyngeal (receptive oral) and rectal (receptive anal) swabs is recommended; extra-genital sampling should be routine in all MSM. Samples may be pooled for testing.
w: Wrong - Omits extra-genital swabs and hepatitis B/C testing despite his blood-borne virus risk.
Wrong - Pharyngeal and rectal infections are often asymptomatic and would be missed by urine alone.
Wrong - Blood tests for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis are an essential part of the screen.
Correct - Full BBV serology plus urine, rectal and pharyngeal CT/NG NAAT matches his exposures.
Wrong - A urethral Gram stain is unhelpful in asymptomatic men and misses extra-genital sites.

mcq.stem:
A medical officer at a Klinik Kesihatan reviews this week's laboratory-confirmed diagnoses before completing notifications to the District Health Office.
Which of the following confirmed diagnoses does NOT require notification under Act 342?
o: Early latent syphilis in a 32-year-old man
Chlamydial urethritis in a 22-year-old man
Gonococcal cervicitis in a 25-year-old woman
Chancroid in a 40-year-old long-distance lorry driver
HIV infection in a 29-year-old man
mcq.e: Only four STIs are among the 31 notifiable diseases under the Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases Act 1988 (Act 342): syphilis, gonorrhoea, HIV and chancroid. Confirmed cases are notified to the nearest District Health Office within 7 days by e-notification or form. Adult genital chlamydia is not notifiable, although the guideline lists gonococcal or chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum as notifiable.
w: Wrong - Confirmed acquired syphilis must be notified (the stage may be stated on the form).
Correct - Adult genital chlamydia is not one of the four notifiable STIs.
Wrong - Laboratory-confirmed gonorrhoea is notifiable within 7 days.
Wrong - Chancroid is one of the four notifiable STIs.
Wrong - Confirmed HIV infection must be notified within 7 days.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old married man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with dysuria. He paid for sex with a female sex worker 4 months ago; he does not inject drugs and has no male partners. Urethral discharge is not confirmed on examination.
Which blood tests should be offered as part of his STI screen?
o: HIV Ag/Ab only, as syphilis is unlikely without an ulcer
HIV Ag/Ab and RPR/TPPA only, as he has no MSM or drug risk
RPR/TPPA only; HIV testing needs a separate counselling visit
No blood tests are indicated today
HIV Ag/Ab, RPR/TPPA, HBsAg and anti-HCV
mcq.e: All heterosexual men are screened for HIV Ag/Ab and syphilis (RPR/VDRL plus a treponemal test). HBsAg and anti-HCV are added when there is blood-borne virus risk, which includes having paid for or been paid for sex. The urethral discharge flowchart still offers HIV, hepatitis B, C and syphilis screening even when discharge is not confirmed.
w: Wrong - Syphilis serology is part of every STI screen; latent syphilis has no ulcer.
Wrong - Paying for sex is a listed blood-borne virus risk, so hepatitis B and C tests are indicated.
Wrong - HIV screening should be offered at the same visit, not deferred.
Wrong - The flowchart offers HIV, hepatitis B, C and syphilis screening even when discharge is not confirmed.
Correct - Paid sex is a BBV risk, so HBsAg and anti-HCV are added to HIV and syphilis serology.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old transwoman who has had vaginoplasty attends for a sexual health check. She reports receptive neovaginal and receptive anal sex with male partners and no oral sex. She is asymptomatic.
Which specimens should be collected for chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT?
o: Neovaginal swab and rectal swab
First-pass urine and rectal swab
First-pass urine sample alone
Neovaginal swab and pharyngeal swab
No NAAT unless she develops symptoms
mcq.e: Transgender people are screened according to their sexual behaviour. For transwomen with a neovagina a urine sample is preferred over a neovaginal swab, and anyone having receptive anal sex should give a rectal swab. Transmen with a vagina who have vaginal sex give a vaginal swab instead of urine.
w: Wrong - In transwomen with a neovagina, urine is preferred rather than a neovaginal swab.
Correct - Urine is preferred for the neovagina, and receptive anal sex requires a rectal swab.
Wrong - Urine alone misses rectal infection from receptive anal sex.
Wrong - Pharyngeal swabs are guided by receptive oral sex, which she denies; urine is preferred to a neovaginal swab.
Wrong - Screening is based on behaviour, not symptoms; most rectal infections are asymptomatic.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man with a genital ulcer was given same-day syndromic treatment at a Klinik Kesihatan and asked to return. At the 7-day review he has taken all medication and his partner has been treated, but the ulcer has not healed and is no smaller.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer to a dermatologist or ID physician
Repeat the same regimen for a further 7 days
Switch empirically to acyclovir 400mg q8h for 10 days
Reassure and review again in 14 days
Add metronidazole 400mg q12h for 7 days
mcq.e: In the anogenital ulcer flowchart the patient returns in 7 days. If the ulcer has healed or is improving, treatment is reviewed and modified according to results; if it is neither healed nor improving, the patient is referred to a dermatologist or ID physician. A persistent ulcer may reflect another aetiology (e.g. donovanosis, neoplasia, HIV-related ulcer) or resistance and needs specialist work-up.
w: Correct - A non-healing, non-improving ulcer at 7 days triggers referral to a dermatologist/ID physician.
Wrong - Repeating an ineffective regimen delays diagnosis of an alternative cause.
Wrong - Blind switching is not the flowchart step; the cause needs specialist evaluation.
Wrong - Further waiting is inappropriate when there is no improvement.
Wrong - Metronidazole does not cover any of the anogenital ulcer pathogens.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old man weighing 160kg presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of purulent urethral discharge and dysuria. Discharge is confirmed on examination. He has no drug allergies and laboratory results will take a week.
What is the most appropriate same-day treatment?
o: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT plus azithromycin 1g PO STAT
Gentamicin 240mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 2g PO STAT
Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 1g PO STAT
mcq.e: For urethral discharge syndrome the preferred regimen covers gonorrhoea and chlamydia: ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg q12h for 7 days. The ceftriaxone dose is increased to 1g when body weight exceeds 150kg. Gentamicin plus azithromycin 2g is the alternative (e.g. cephalosporin allergy) and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin 1g is the pregnancy regimen.
w: Wrong - Correct drugs, but body weight above 150kg requires ceftriaxone 1g.
Wrong - Azithromycin 1g replaces doxycycline only in pregnancy.
Wrong - Gentamicin plus azithromycin 2g is the alternative for those who cannot have ceftriaxone.
Correct - Weight >150kg: ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg q12h for 7 days.
Wrong - This is the pregnancy regimen, and it under-doses ceftriaxone for his weight.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man returns 2 weeks after receiving ceftriaxone 500mg IM plus a 7-day course of doxycycline for urethral discharge. He completed the course, has had no sexual contact since and his only partner was treated. Discharge is still present on milking the urethra.
What is the most appropriate treatment now?
o: Repeat ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg q12h for a further 7 days
Metronidazole 5 days plus moxifloxacin 400mg daily for 10–14 days
Metronidazole 5 days plus azithromycin 500mg STAT then 250mg daily for 4 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 21 days
Acyclovir 400mg PO q8h for 7–10 days
mcq.e: Persistent discharge without reinfection or poor compliance is treated for Trichomonas vaginalis and Mycoplasma genitalium. Metronidazole 400mg q12h for 5 days covers TV; for M. genitalium the choice depends on the first-line drug: after doxycycline give extended azithromycin (500mg STAT, then 250mg daily for 4 days), after azithromycin give moxifloxacin 400mg daily for 10–14 days. Repeating standard treatment is only for reinfection or poor adherence.
w: Wrong - Repeat standard treatment is reserved for reinfection or poor compliance, both excluded here.
Wrong - Moxifloxacin is chosen when azithromycin, not doxycycline, was the first-line drug.
Correct - After doxycycline first line: metronidazole plus extended azithromycin covers TV and M. genitalium.
Wrong - A 21-day doxycycline course treats LGV, not persistent urethritis.
Wrong - HSV is an uncommon cause of urethritis and does not explain persistent discharge here.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with 1 week of increased white vaginal discharge and vulval itch. She has no lower abdominal pain or tenderness and declines a vaginal examination after counselling. Her only partner is her husband.
What is the most appropriate same-day treatment?
o: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg q12h for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT, then doxycycline plus metronidazole for 14 days
Fluconazole 150mg PO STAT alone, with no further review
Metronidazole 400mg q12h for 7 days for her and her husband
Clotrimazole 500mg pessary STAT plus metronidazole 400mg q12h 5–7 days
mcq.e: When a woman with vaginal discharge declines examination and has no lower abdominal tenderness, the risk-assessment flowchart gives same-day treatment for candidiasis and bacterial vaginosis: clotrimazole 500mg pessary STAT plus metronidazole 400mg q12h for 5–7 days, with review in 14 days. Cervicitis (gonorrhoea/chlamydia) is treated when mucopurulent cervical discharge is seen on speculum examination, and PID treatment needs lower abdominal or cervical motion tenderness.
w: Wrong - Gonorrhoea/chlamydia cover is given for cervical mucopurulent discharge seen on speculum examination.
Wrong - The PID regimen requires lower abdominal or cervical motion tenderness, which is absent.
Wrong - The flowchart covers both candidiasis and BV and reviews the patient in 14 days.
Wrong - Partner treatment is not needed for BV or candidiasis, and candida is left uncovered.
Correct - Same-day cover for candidiasis and bacterial vaginosis per the risk-assessment flowchart.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of lower abdominal pain and vaginal discharge. Her period is 2 weeks overdue. She has cervical excitation tenderness; there is no guarding, BP is 118/72 mmHg and pulse 88/min.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start outpatient PID treatment and review in 3 days
Refer for gynaecological assessment after setting up an IV line
Treat for cervicitis with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline; review in 14 days
Treat for candidiasis and BV and review in 14 days
Reassure and repeat abdominal examination in 1 week
mcq.e: In the lower abdominal pain flowchart, any of the following mandates referral for surgical/gynaecological assessment: pregnancy, missed or overdue period, recent delivery/abortion/miscarriage, guarding or rebound, abnormal vaginal bleeding, abdominal mass or abnormal vital signs. An IV line and resuscitation are set up before transfer. Only women without these flags are managed as PID with review at 3 days, because ectopic pregnancy must be excluded first.
w: Wrong - A missed period is a red flag; ectopic pregnancy must be excluded before outpatient PID treatment.
Correct - Overdue period: refer for gynaecological opinion, with IV access set up before transfer.
Wrong - Cervicitis treatment does not address the possibility of ectopic pregnancy.
Wrong - Candidiasis/BV does not explain cervical excitation tenderness, and the red flag is ignored.
Wrong - Delay is dangerous when an ectopic pregnancy has not been excluded.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old man who has receptive anal sex presents with 4 days of severe perianal pain. Examination shows several shallow, very tender perianal ulcers; there is no rectal discharge. He feels feverish.
In addition to screening for HIV, hepatitis B, C and syphilis, which treatment should be considered?
o: Acyclovir 400mg PO q8h for 7–10 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 21 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline for 7 days
Azithromycin 1g PO STAT
Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM STAT
mcq.e: In the anorectal syndrome flowchart, anal or perianal pain with an ulcer prompts treatment for herpes simplex. Multiple shallow, very painful ulcers with systemic symptoms are typical of a first episode of HSV, treated with acyclovir 400mg q8h for 7–10 days. Same-day gonorrhoea/chlamydia treatment is given when there is anal discharge, and LGV treatment is considered if discharge persists at 7 days.
w: Correct - Painful perianal ulcers in the anorectal flowchart prompt treatment for herpes simplex.
Wrong - 21-day doxycycline is for LGV, considered when rectal discharge persists.
Wrong - Gonorrhoea/chlamydia treatment is triggered by anal discharge, which is absent.
Wrong - Azithromycin 1g STAT treats chancroid, whose ulcers are typically genital with buboes.
Wrong - Syphilitic chancres are usually painless; multiple very painful ulcers suggest HSV.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man who has sex with men had purulent rectal discharge and tenesmus 1 week ago and was given ceftriaxone 500mg IM plus doxycycline 100mg q12h for 7 days. He completed treatment, but the haemopurulent discharge and rectal pain persist. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy.
What is the most appropriate treatment now?
o: Repeat ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 7 days
Metronidazole 400mg PO q12h for 5 days
Acyclovir 400mg PO q8h for 7–10 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 21 days
Gentamicin 240mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 2g PO STAT
mcq.e: If rectal discharge persists at the 7-day review of the anorectal syndrome flowchart, LGV should be considered and treated with doxycycline 100mg q12h for 21 days (alternatives: azithromycin 1g weekly for 3 weeks or erythromycin 800mg q6h for 21 days). LGV proctitis in MSM causes haemopurulent discharge, severe pain and tenesmus, usually without inguinal nodes. A positive chlamydia NAAT should be sent for LGV genotyping.
w: Wrong - Repeating the 7-day regimen under-treats invasive LGV serovars.
Wrong - Metronidazole does not treat chlamydial LGV proctitis.
Wrong - HSV is considered when there is anal pain with ulcers, not persistent discharge.
Correct - Persistent rectal discharge: treat for LGV with 21 days of doxycycline.
Wrong - This is the alternative regimen for gonorrhoea, not a treatment for LGV.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man presents with a 5-day-old solitary, painless, indurated ulcer on the coronal sulcus with rubbery, non-tender inguinal nodes. Syphilis RDT and RPR are non-reactive and TPPA is negative. HSV PCR is pending.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure him that negative serology excludes syphilis
Treat with acyclovir only and await the HSV PCR result
Repeat syphilis serology in 3 months before deciding on treatment
Arrange lumbar puncture to look for neurosyphilis
Give benzathine penicillin now and repeat serology in 2 weeks
mcq.e: Serology can still be negative in early primary syphilis. If there is clinical suspicion of a chancre, give presumptive treatment and repeat serology after 2 weeks; a T. pallidum PCR swab of the lesion can help. Any anogenital ulcer should be considered syphilis until proven otherwise.
w: Wrong - Serology may not yet be positive in early primary syphilis.
Wrong - A painless indurated ulcer is classically syphilitic; acyclovir alone leaves syphilis untreated.
Wrong - Delaying treatment allows progression and onward transmission.
Wrong - There are no neurological features; CSF examination is not indicated.
Correct - Presumptive treatment and repeat serology after 2 weeks (consider lesion PCR).

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has routine pre-operative blood tests. Her RPR is reactive at 1:2 and her TPPA is negative. She has been married for 20 years and reports no other sexual partners or risk exposure.
What is the most likely interpretation?
o: Early latent syphilis
Late latent syphilis
Biological false-positive RPR
Previously treated syphilis with a serofast titre
Prozone phenomenon masking a high titre
mcq.e: In the traditional algorithm a reactive non-treponemal test with a negative treponemal test means syphilis is unlikely and suggests a biological false positive, seen with autoimmune disease, pregnancy and other infections. Treated or untreated syphilis gives a positive TPPA, which normally stays positive for life. If she were at risk, the tests would be repeated in 2–4 weeks.
w: Wrong - Any true syphilis stage would have a positive treponemal test.
Wrong - Late latent syphilis also requires a positive treponemal test.
Correct - RPR reactive with TPPA negative is a biological false positive; syphilis is unlikely.
Wrong - Previously treated syphilis still leaves the TPPA positive.
Wrong - Prozone causes a falsely negative RPR, not a negative TPPA.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old man has a 3-week generalised non-itchy papulosquamous rash involving the palms and soles, moist flat plaques around the anus and patchy alopecia. CMIA and TPPA are both reactive but the RPR is reported as non-reactive. He has never been treated for syphilis.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask the laboratory to repeat the RPR on diluted serum
Report a biological false-positive treponemal result
Treat as late latent syphilis with weekly benzathine for 3 weeks
Repeat both tests in 3 months before deciding
Refer for skin biopsy to exclude psoriasis
mcq.e: Untreated secondary syphilis is expected to give positive results on all serological tests, usually with an RPR titre above 1:8. A non-reactive RPR with florid secondary signs suggests the prozone phenomenon, in which a very high antibody concentration prevents flocculation; diluting the serum reveals the true high titre. He still needs treatment for early syphilis (single benzathine 2.4MU dose), and the titre is needed as the baseline for follow-up.
w: Correct - Diluting the serum overcomes the prozone effect and gives the true baseline titre.
Wrong - Two positive treponemal tests with classic secondary signs are not a false positive.
Wrong - Secondary syphilis is early syphilis and needs a single benzathine dose, not 3 weekly doses.
Wrong - Delay is inappropriate in an infectious patient with classic features.
Wrong - Palmoplantar rash, condylomata lata and patchy alopecia with positive treponemal tests indicate secondary syphilis.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man is found on screening to have RPR 1:16 and a positive TPPA. He is asymptomatic with a normal examination. His RPR and TPPA were both non-reactive at a blood donation 18 months ago. He has no drug allergy.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 weeks
Benzylpenicillin 4MU IV q4h for 14 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 28 days
Procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for 14 days
Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM as a single dose
mcq.e: Positive serology without signs in someone seronegative within the previous 2 years is early latent syphilis, treated like primary and secondary syphilis with a single dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM (or procaine 600,000 units daily for 10 days). Three weekly doses, 14 days of procaine or 28 days of doxycycline are late syphilis regimens, and IV benzylpenicillin is for neurosyphilis.
w: Wrong - Weekly doses for 3 weeks are for late latent or unknown-duration syphilis.
Wrong - IV benzylpenicillin is reserved for neurosyphilis, including ocular and otosyphilis.
Wrong - 28 days of doxycycline is the late syphilis regimen for penicillin allergy.
Wrong - Procaine for 14 days is the late syphilis alternative; early syphilis needs 10 days.
Correct - Seroconversion within 2 years = early latent syphilis: a single benzathine 2.4MU IM dose.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man with asymptomatic syphilis of unknown duration (RPR 1:8, TPPA positive, normal examination) is on benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly. He received his first and second doses a week apart, then returns 3 weeks after the second dose because he was travelling.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the third dose today to complete the course
Restart the full course of three weekly doses
Give two further weekly doses, starting today
Stop injections; recheck RPR in 3 months
Switch to doxycycline 100mg PO q12h for 14 days
mcq.e: Syphilis of unknown duration is managed as late latent syphilis: benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 doses. If a patient defaults for 2 weeks or more between the weekly doses, the whole regimen must be restarted. Shorter delays allow the course to continue.
w: Wrong - The gap is too long; the course cannot simply be completed.
Correct - A default of 2 weeks or more between weekly doses requires restarting all three doses.
Wrong - Adding doses does not fix the gap; the whole regimen must be restarted.
Wrong - Two doses are incomplete treatment for late latent syphilis.
Wrong - 14 days of doxycycline is the early syphilis allergy regimen, and he has no allergy.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man was treated with benzathine penicillin for secondary syphilis 3 months ago (baseline RPR 1:32). His rash has resolved. Today the RPR is 1:8 and the TPPA remains positive, which worries him.
What is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?
o: Treatment failure; retreat with weekly benzathine for 3 weeks
Probable reinfection; give a further single dose of benzathine
Possible neurosyphilis; arrange lumbar puncture
Adequate response; repeat RPR at 6 and 12 months
Cured; discharge as the RPR has fallen
mcq.e: Response is judged by the non-treponemal titre: a fourfold (two-dilution) fall, here 1:32 to 1:8, is an adequate response. RPR is repeated at 3, 6 and 12 months, then 6-monthly until negative or serofast. Treponemal tests such as TPPA usually stay positive for life and must not be used to monitor treatment.
w: Wrong - A persistently positive TPPA is expected and is not a sign of failure.
Wrong - Reinfection would cause a rising, not falling, RPR titre.
Wrong - A falling titre without neurological signs does not warrant CSF examination.
Correct - A fourfold RPR fall is adequate; continue RPR follow-up at 6 and 12 months.
Wrong - Follow-up continues until RPR is negative or serofast; one fall is not discharge.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man was treated with benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM for primary syphilis 12 months ago (RPR 1:16). He reports no new sexual partners and his partner was treated. He is asymptomatic and HIV negative, but his RPR today is still 1:16.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give a further single dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM
Label him serofast and discharge from follow-up
Arrange CSF examination to exclude neurosyphilis
Repeat TPPA to confirm ongoing infection
Treat his partner again and recheck RPR in 6 months
mcq.e: Failure of the RPR to fall fourfold by 1 year (or a sustained fourfold rise, or persistent signs) means treatment failure. If reinfection is excluded, CSF examination is done; if neurosyphilis is excluded, retreat with benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 weeks. A serofast state applies only after an appropriate fall to a low, stable titre.
w: Wrong - Retreatment is three weekly doses, and only after neurosyphilis has been excluded.
Wrong - Serofast follows an adequate fall; an unchanged 1:16 at 1 year is treatment failure.
Correct - Treatment failure without reinfection requires CSF examination before retreatment.
Wrong - TPPA remains positive after treatment and gives no information on disease activity.
Wrong - Reinfection is unlikely; the patient himself needs evaluation for treatment failure.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man has a reactive syphilis RDT at a health screening in a Klinik Kesihatan. His RPR is 1:4 and TPPA is positive. He has never been tested before and cannot recall any genital ulcer or rash. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations are normal. He has no drug allergy.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM as a single dose
Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 doses
Benzylpenicillin 4MU IV 4-hourly for 14 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 14 days
Procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for 10 days
mcq.e: Positive serology without symptoms and no negative test in the previous 2 years is **late latent syphilis** (unknown duration is treated as late). The regimen is **benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 weeks (3 doses)**. A single dose is only for early syphilis (< 2 years), and IV benzylpenicillin is reserved for neurosyphilis.
w: Wrong - A single dose treats early syphilis only; unknown duration is managed as late latent.
Correct - Late latent or unknown-duration syphilis needs 3 weekly doses of benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM.
Wrong - IV benzylpenicillin is for neurosyphilis; his neurological examination is normal.
Wrong - Doxycycline is only for penicillin allergy, and late syphilis needs 28 days, not 14.
Wrong - Procaine penicillin is an alternative for late syphilis but is given for 14 days, not 10.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a non-itchy rash on his trunk, palms and soles and generalised lymphadenopathy for 3 weeks. RPR is 1:64 and TPPA is positive. Two years ago he developed facial swelling and wheeze after amoxicillin. He has no neurological or eye symptoms.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Azithromycin 2g PO as a single dose
Erythromycin 500mg PO 6-hourly for 14 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 28 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 14 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM daily for 10 days
mcq.e: This is **secondary syphilis**, which is early syphilis. For a non-pregnant adult with penicillin allergy the guideline alternative is **doxycycline 100mg 12-hourly for 14 days**; the 28-day course is for late latent, gummatous or cardiovascular syphilis. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin appear only as fallback options in pregnancy after failed desensitisation.
w: Wrong - Azithromycin 2g is listed only for pregnant women after failed penicillin desensitisation.
Wrong - Erythromycin is not a guideline regimen for early syphilis in non-pregnant adults.
Wrong - 28 days of doxycycline is the duration for late syphilis, not early syphilis.
Correct - Early syphilis with penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100mg 12-hourly for 14 days.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone 500mg daily for 10 days is the pregnancy fallback after failed desensitisation.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old HIV-negative man with a reactive RPR (1:32) and positive TPPA presents with headache and a new right lower motor neurone facial palsy. Lumbar puncture shows CSF WBC 14 cells/μL, protein 0.62 g/L and a non-reactive CSF VDRL. He has no drug allergy.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Benzylpenicillin 4MU IV 4-hourly for 14 days
Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 doses
Benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM as a single dose
Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 28 days
Repeat the lumbar puncture in 3 months first
mcq.e: In an HIV-negative patient, CSF WBC > 5/μL and protein > 0.45 g/L meet the **neurosyphilis** criteria; a negative CSF VDRL makes neurosyphilis less likely but **does not exclude it**, especially with a cranial nerve palsy. Treatment is **benzylpenicillin 4MU IV 4-hourly for 14 days** (or procaine penicillin 2.4MU IM daily plus probenecid for 14 days). Benzathine penicillin does not reliably reach treponemicidal CSF levels.
w: Correct - CSF pleocytosis and raised protein with a cranial nerve palsy: treat neurosyphilis with IV benzylpenicillin for 14 days.
Wrong - Weekly benzathine is for late latent, gummatous and cardiovascular syphilis, not CNS disease.
Wrong - A single benzathine dose is for early syphilis without CNS involvement.
Wrong - Doxycycline is only for penicillin anaphylaxis in neurosyphilis, at 200mg 12-hourly for 28 days.
Wrong - A negative CSF VDRL does not exclude neurosyphilis; delay risks permanent deficit.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman, not pregnant, receives benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM for secondary syphilis at a Klinik Kesihatan. Eight hours later she phones the clinic with fever of 38.6°C, rigors, headache and aching joints. She has no wheeze, lip swelling or breathlessness, and her rash looks slightly redder.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Attend for adrenaline 0.5mg IM and admission
Record a penicillin allergy and switch to doxycycline
Start prednisolone 40mg daily for the next 3 days
Attend for a lumbar puncture to exclude neurosyphilis
Take paracetamol; it should settle within 24 hours
mcq.e: Fever, rigors, headache and arthralgia 6-12 hours after the first dose is the **Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction**, caused by release of treponemal products as organisms are killed. It is common in early syphilis, **resolves within 24 hours** and is reduced by antipyretics. It is not an allergy; it matters mainly in pregnancy (foetal distress, preterm labour) and with neurological, ophthalmic or cardiovascular involvement.
w: Wrong - There are no airway, breathing or circulatory features of anaphylaxis.
Wrong - JHR is not an allergy; a false allergy label removes the best drug for future treatment.
Wrong - Prednisolone is considered only for cardiovascular and neurosyphilis, starting before antibiotics.
Wrong - Fever and headache here are an expected treatment reaction with no neurological signs.
Correct - This is JHR: antipyretics and reassurance, as it resolves within 24 hours.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with secondary syphilis at a Klinik Kesihatan. His rash began 2 months ago. He had a non-reactive syphilis test 3 years ago and has had several casual partners since then.
According to the guideline, how far back should his sexual partners be traced?
o: 3 months plus the duration of symptoms
The last 60 days before the diagnosis
6 months plus the duration of symptoms
12 months or to the most recent negative test
Back to his last non-reactive test 3 years ago
mcq.e: Look-back depends on stage: **primary** 3 months plus symptom duration, **secondary 6 months plus symptom duration**, **early latent** 12 months (or to the most recent negative test). The 60-day window applies to gonorrhoea, chlamydia and NGU. A last negative test only shortens the window when it is more recent than the stage-based period.
w: Wrong - 3 months plus symptom duration is the look-back for primary syphilis.
Wrong - 60 days is the look-back for gonorrhoea, chlamydia and NGU.
Correct - Secondary syphilis: trace partners from 6 months plus the duration of symptoms.
Wrong - 12 months applies to early latent syphilis.
Wrong - A negative test 3 years ago is far outside the early syphilis look-back window.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman, not pregnant, attends a Klinik Kesihatan because her husband was diagnosed with primary syphilis yesterday. They last had sex 3 weeks ago. She is well, examination is normal, and her syphilis RDT and RPR today are non-reactive. She has no drug allergy.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Give benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM today
Reassure and repeat her serology in 3 months
Treat only if repeat serology in 2-4 weeks is reactive
Give benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM weekly for 3 doses
Give doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 28 days
mcq.e: Contacts within **90 days** of an early syphilis diagnosis may be incubating infection while still seronegative, so they are **treated epidemiologically even if serology is negative**. Epidemiological treatment is benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM stat (doxycycline 100mg 12-hourly for 14 days if allergic). Contacts beyond 90 days are treated if results are not immediately available and follow-up is uncertain.
w: Correct - A contact within 90 days gets epidemiological benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM stat despite negative serology.
Wrong - Negative serology does not exclude incubating syphilis after a recent exposure.
Wrong - Waiting risks progression and onward transmission; she is treated now regardless.
Wrong - Three weekly doses are for late syphilis; incubating syphilis needs a single dose.
Wrong - Doxycycline is for penicillin allergy, and only 14 days for incubating syphilis.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old primigravida at 12 weeks attends her booking visit at a Klinik Kesihatan. Her syphilis rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is positive. She is asymptomatic, has no drug allergy and has never been screened before.
What is the most appropriate next step at this visit?
o: Send blood for RPR and treat once the titre is known
Refer to the hospital O&G clinic before any treatment
Repeat the RDT at 28 weeks to confirm the result
Give benzathine 2.4MU IM now and send blood for RPR
Start oral erythromycin and send blood for a TPPA
mcq.e: The MOH antenatal RDT flow chart (WHO strategy C) says a **positive RDT** is referred to the FMS/MO the same day to **start the first dose of benzathine penicillin and send blood for RPR**. Treating at first contact prevents loss to follow-up and vertical transmission; confirmation and staging then decide whether the 2nd and 3rd doses are needed, with hospital specialist referral for delivery.
w: Wrong - Waiting for results risks losing her to follow-up; the first dose is given at this visit.
Wrong - She is referred to hospital later, but treatment starts in the clinic today.
Wrong - 28-32 weeks is the repeat screen for RDT-negative mothers, not confirmation of a positive.
Correct - Positive antenatal RDT: give the first benzathine dose and send RPR on the same visit.
Wrong - Erythromycin does not reliably treat the foetus; penicillin is the only proven drug.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old woman at 16 weeks received benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM at her booking visit after a positive syphilis RDT. Her RPR returns at 1:4 and TPPA is positive. She has never been tested before, recalls no ulcer or rash, and is asymptomatic.
What is the most appropriate further treatment?
o: No further antibiotic; repeat the RPR monthly
Two more weekly doses of benzathine 2.4MU IM
Benzylpenicillin 4MU IV 4-hourly for 14 days
Erythromycin 800mg PO 6-hourly for 28 days
One repeat dose of benzathine penicillin at 28 weeks
mcq.e: Infection of **unknown duration** is managed as late latent syphilis, so she needs the **2nd and 3rd weekly doses** to complete three. The flow chart also gives the extra doses for known late latent syphilis and for syphilis treated more than 2 years ago with a current 4-fold titre rise. A low RPR titre does not prove early or past treated infection.
w: Wrong - One dose is adequate only for early syphilis; her duration is unknown.
Correct - Unknown-duration syphilis in pregnancy: complete 3 weekly doses of benzathine penicillin.
Wrong - IV benzylpenicillin is for neurosyphilis; she has no neurological features.
Wrong - Erythromycin is only for penicillin allergy and does not adequately treat the foetus.
Wrong - Doses must be weekly; a gap of 2 weeks or more means restarting the course.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks has secondary syphilis (RPR 1:32, TPPA positive). Five years ago she developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling and hypotension within minutes of an IM penicillin injection. She has no asthma or cardiac disease.
What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 14 days
Azithromycin 2g PO as a single dose today
Erythromycin 800mg PO 6-hourly for 28 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM daily for 10 days now
Penicillin desensitisation, then benzathine
mcq.e: **Penicillin G is the only drug proven to prevent vertical transmission and treat the foetus**, so a pregnant woman with true IgE-mediated allergy is **desensitised** (HDU/ICU, obstetric team on standby, foetal monitoring) and then treated with penicillin. Ceftriaxone or azithromycin are used only if desensitisation fails, and if a macrolide is used the baby needs assessment and treatment at birth. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
w: Wrong - Doxycycline and tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - Azithromycin is a fallback only after failed desensitisation and does not reliably treat the foetus.
Wrong - Erythromycin is the late-syphilis allergy option and crosses the placenta poorly.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone is reserved for failed desensitisation, not first choice.
Correct - IgE-mediated allergy in pregnancy: desensitise and treat with penicillin.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old woman at 30 weeks receives benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM for early syphilis at a Klinik Kesihatan. Her RPR is 1:64.
Which advice is most important before she leaves the clinic?
o: Avoid paracetamol, as it may mask a drug allergy
Her next antenatal check can wait until 36 weeks
Return urgently if contractions or fewer foetal kicks
Her RPR and TPPA should be negative by delivery
She should not breastfeed after the delivery
mcq.e: The **Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction** occurs 6-12 hours after treatment, especially in early syphilis with high titres, and in pregnancy it may cause **foetal distress and premature labour**. Mothers are told to seek care for any change in foetal movements or contractions. Follow-up is **monthly clinical and serological review until delivery**, with RPR repeated at delivery.
w: Wrong - Antipyretics reduce the reaction; JHR is not an allergy.
Wrong - She needs monthly clinical and serological review until delivery.
Correct - JHR in pregnancy can trigger preterm labour or foetal distress, so she must return urgently.
Wrong - The TPPA usually stays positive for life; the RPR is expected to fall, not necessarily vanish.
Wrong - Treated syphilis is not a reason to avoid breastfeeding.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman at 18 weeks has early latent syphilis. Three years ago she was admitted to ICU with Stevens-Johnson syndrome after taking amoxicillin. She has no other medical problems.
What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Oral penicillin desensitisation in HDU, then benzathine
Penicillin skin test; if negative, give benzathine
Non-penicillin option; IV penicillin for baby at birth
Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 14 days
Defer all treatment until after the delivery
mcq.e: Oral penicillin desensitisation is **absolutely contraindicated** after confirmed life-threatening non-immediate reactions (**SJS/TEN, DRESS**), non-IgE reactions, unstable vital signs, poorly controlled asthma or uncontrolled cardiac disease. These women receive an alternative appropriate to the stage, chosen with the ID physician and obstetrician, and **the newborn must be given IV penicillin immediately after delivery**. Desensitisation only induces temporary tolerance of IgE-mediated allergy.
w: Wrong - Desensitisation is absolutely contraindicated after penicillin-induced SJS.
Wrong - Skin tests do not predict T-cell reactions such as SJS, and re-exposure is dangerous.
Correct - SJS history: treat with an alternative and give the baby IV penicillin immediately after birth.
Wrong - Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - Deferring treatment allows vertical transmission and stillbirth.

mcq.stem:
A term baby is born at a district hospital. The mother was adequately treated with benzathine penicillin for syphilis 4 years before this pregnancy, and her RPR stayed at 1:2 throughout pregnancy and at delivery with no new exposure. The baby's examination is normal and the baby's RPR is 1:2.
How should this baby be classified?
o: Confirmed congenital syphilis
Congenital syphilis unlikely
Highly probable congenital syphilis
Possible congenital syphilis
Congenital syphilis less likely
mcq.e: A normal baby with a titre no more than fourfold the mother's, whose mother was **adequately treated before pregnancy** and stayed **serofast at a low titre** (VDRL ≤ 1:2 or RPR ≤ 1:4), is **congenital syphilis unlikely**. No evaluation or treatment is required, but a reactive baby is followed serologically until the RPR is negative. 'Less likely' applies when the mother was treated during pregnancy, at least 30 days before delivery.
w: Wrong - Nothing here confirms infection; the baby's titre equals the mother's passively transferred antibody.
Correct - Adequate treatment before pregnancy plus a low stable maternal titre: congenital syphilis unlikely.
Wrong - Highly probable needs abnormal signs, a fourfold higher titre or untreated maternal syphilis.
Wrong - Possible applies when maternal treatment was absent, inadequate, non-penicillin or < 30 days before delivery.
Wrong - Less likely applies when the mother was treated during this pregnancy.

mcq.stem:
A 3-day-old baby is born to a mother whose syphilis was first detected at delivery and was untreated (RPR 1:4). The baby has hepatosplenomegaly, snuffles and a desquamating rash on the palms and soles. The baby's RPR is 1:32. CSF results are pending.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Benzathine penicillin 50,000 units/kg IM single dose
Ceftriaxone 100mg/kg IM daily for 10-14 days
No treatment yet; repeat RPR at 3 months of age
Benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg IV for 10-14 days
Procaine penicillin 50,000 units/kg IM single dose
mcq.e: Abnormal examination, a titre fourfold above the mother's and untreated maternal syphilis each make congenital syphilis **highly probable**; this baby has all three. Treatment is **benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg/dose IV 12-hourly for the first 7 days of life, then 8-hourly to complete 10-14 days** (procaine penicillin 50,000 units/kg IM daily for 10-14 days is the alternative). If any dose is missed for 1 day or more, the whole course is restarted.
w: Wrong - A single benzathine dose is for the less likely group, not active disease.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone 100mg/kg is the alternative for babies 30 days or older; this baby is 3 days old.
Wrong - A symptomatic baby with a fourfold higher titre needs treatment now.
Correct - Highly probable congenital syphilis: IV benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg for 10-14 days.
Wrong - Procaine penicillin is given daily for 10-14 days, never as a single dose.

mcq.stem:
A healthy term baby is born to a mother diagnosed with early latent syphilis at 14 weeks, who received benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM at that visit. Her RPR fell from 1:32 to 1:4 by delivery with no evidence of reinfection. The baby's examination is normal and the RPR is 1:2.
What is the most appropriate management of the baby?
o: Benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg IM single dose
Full evaluation with LP, long bone and chest X-rays
IV benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg for 10-14 days
No treatment and discharge from follow-up at birth
Ceftriaxone 75mg/kg IM daily for 10-14 days
mcq.e: Stage-appropriate penicillin started **at least 30 days before delivery**, an adequate fall in titre, no reinfection, and a normal baby with a titre not more than fourfold the mother's = **congenital syphilis less likely**. No evaluation is needed; give **benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg IM as a single dose**. A reactive baby still needs serological follow-up until the RPR becomes negative.
w: Correct - Less likely congenital syphilis: single IM benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg, no evaluation.
Wrong - Full evaluation is for babies of untreated, inadequately or recently treated mothers.
Wrong - A 10-14 day IV course is for confirmed or highly probable disease.
Wrong - The less likely group is treated, and a reactive baby needs serological follow-up.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone is an alternative for treating active congenital syphilis, not this low-risk baby.

mcq.stem:
A term baby is born at a district hospital. The mother was diagnosed with secondary syphilis at 37 weeks and received benzathine penicillin 2.4MU IM 12 days before delivery. The baby looks well and maternal RPR at delivery is 1:32.
What is the most appropriate next step for the baby?
o: Discharge, as the mother received penicillin
Single benzathine dose without further follow-up
Repeat the RPR at 3 months and treat if rising
Check the baby's TPPA and treat only if positive
Full evaluation: RPR, CSF, long bone and chest X-rays
mcq.e: Maternal treatment started **less than 30 days (1 month) before delivery** is not considered protective, so the baby is at least possible congenital syphilis and must be **evaluated**: thorough examination, RPR compared with the mother's, CSF cells, protein and VDRL, long bone X-rays and chest X-ray. Treatment follows the findings. A baby's TPPA reflects passively transferred maternal IgG and cannot guide this decision.
w: Wrong - Penicillin given < 30 days before delivery may not have treated the foetus.
Wrong - The baby needs evaluation, and any reactive baby needs serological follow-up.
Wrong - Waiting 3 months risks missing early congenital syphilis in an at-risk baby.
Wrong - Neonatal treponemal antibody is largely maternal IgG and is not used to decide treatment.
Correct - Mother treated < 1 month before delivery: fully evaluate the baby.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man weighing 75kg presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of profuse purulent urethral discharge and dysuria after condomless sex with a casual partner. Urethral Gram stain shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci. Chlamydia testing is not available. He has no allergies.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 250mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 1g PO STAT
Ciprofloxacin 500mg PO STAT plus doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days
Gentamicin 240mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 2g PO STAT
Cefixime 400mg PO STAT plus doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days
mcq.e: Uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea is treated with **ceftriaxone 500mg IM stat** (1g if weight > 150kg). If chlamydia has not been ruled out, non-pregnant patients also receive **doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days**. Gentamicin 240mg IM plus azithromycin 2g is the alternative (e.g. cephalosporin allergy); quinolones and low-dose cephalosporins are not used because of resistance.
w: Correct - Ceftriaxone 500mg IM stat with doxycycline 7 days when chlamydia is not excluded.
Wrong - 250mg ceftriaxone is an outdated dose that no longer reliably cures gonorrhoea.
Wrong - Gonococcal quinolone resistance is widespread; ciprofloxacin is not recommended.
Wrong - Gentamicin plus azithromycin 2g is the alternative, not first line for a non-allergic man.
Wrong - Oral cefixime is not a guideline regimen, and chlamydia cover is 7 days.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation has mucopurulent cervical discharge. Her endocervical NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae; the chlamydia result is not yet available. She has no drug allergy.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days
Gentamicin 240mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 2g PO STAT
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 1g PO STAT
Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT plus metronidazole 400mg BD for 7 days
Cefixime 400mg PO STAT plus erythromycin 500mg QID for 7 days
mcq.e: **Ceftriaxone 500mg IM stat** is first line in pregnancy as well. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, so chlamydia cover is **azithromycin 1g as a single dose**. Her newborn must be screened for gonorrhoea, and partners from the last 60 days treated epidemiologically.
w: Wrong - Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - Gentamicin is avoided in pregnancy and is only the non-pregnant alternative.
Correct - In pregnancy: ceftriaxone 500mg IM stat plus azithromycin 1g stat for chlamydia cover.
Wrong - Metronidazole covers trichomonas and BV, not chlamydia, and 1g is not the uncomplicated dose.
Wrong - Oral cefixime and erythromycin are not guideline regimens for gonorrhoea.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man who has sex with men has routine NAAT screening at a Klinik Kesihatan. His pharyngeal swab is positive for gonorrhoea; urine and rectal swabs are negative. He is treated with ceftriaxone 500mg IM and remains asymptomatic.
What follow-up testing is recommended?
o: No test of cure; routine screening in 12 months
NAAT test of cure no earlier than 4 weeks after
Gonococcal serology 6 weeks after treatment
Repeat pharyngeal swab only if symptoms appear
Test of cure by culture or NAAT at 7-14 days
mcq.e: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea is harder to eradicate and is a reservoir for resistance, so a **routine test of cure by culture or NAAT 7-14 days after treatment** is recommended; the same applies when a non-first-line regimen was used and susceptibility is unknown. Routine test of cure is not needed for uncomplicated urethral, cervical or rectal infection. The 'not before 4 weeks' rule belongs to chlamydia.
w: Wrong - Pharyngeal infection is an indication for a routine test of cure.
Wrong - The 4-week minimum is the chlamydia test-of-cure rule.
Wrong - Serology has no role in diagnosing gonorrhoea or confirming cure.
Wrong - Pharyngeal gonorrhoea is usually asymptomatic, so symptoms cannot be relied on.
Correct - Pharyngeal gonorrhoea: test of cure by culture or NAAT 7-14 days after treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan because her boyfriend was treated for gonorrhoea 3 days ago. They last had sex a week ago. She has no symptoms; speculum examination is normal and an endocervical Gram stain shows no Gram-negative diplococci. NAAT has been sent.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure her, as a negative Gram stain excludes it
Give ceftriaxone 500mg IM plus doxycycline today
Await the NAAT result and treat only if positive
Repeat the endocervical Gram stain in 2 weeks
Treat only if the gonococcal culture is positive
mcq.e: Endocervical Gram stain detects only **45-65%** of gonorrhoea in women, so a negative smear does not exclude infection. **Partners within the last 60 days are treated epidemiologically irrespective of test results**, with ceftriaxone 500mg IM and chlamydia cover. She should abstain from condomless sex for 7 days after both have been treated.
w: Wrong - Gram stain sensitivity in women is only 45-65%.
Correct - A partner within 60 days is treated epidemiologically regardless of results.
Wrong - Waiting delays treatment of a likely infection and risks PID and onward spread.
Wrong - Repeating an insensitive test does not change management.
Wrong - Epidemiological treatment does not depend on culture results.

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 4 days of fever, migratory joint pains and a painful swollen right wrist with tenderness along the extensor tendons. There are a few small pustules on an erythematous base on her fingers. She has a new sexual partner and mild vaginal discharge. Temperature is 38.4°C.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT and review in 1 week
Oral doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days plus regular NSAIDs
Aspirate the wrist and start oral cloxacillin
Admit for ceftriaxone 1g IV daily for 7 or more days
Refer to rheumatology for reactive arthritis care
mcq.e: Fever, tenosynovitis, migratory polyarthralgia and acral pustules in a sexually active young woman suggest **disseminated gonococcal infection** (arthritis-dermatitis syndrome). DGI needs **hospitalisation and physician input with ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV daily for at least 7 days** (10-14 days with meningitis, 4 weeks with endocarditis). A single 500mg dose treats only uncomplicated mucosal infection.
w: Wrong - A single 500mg dose treats uncomplicated infection, not bacteraemic DGI.
Wrong - Doxycycline covers chlamydia, not disseminated gonococcal infection.
Wrong - Cloxacillin targets staphylococci and misses N. gonorrhoeae.
Correct - DGI: admit for ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV daily for at least 7 days.
Wrong - Fever and pustules point to infection, not reactive arthritis.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man's urine NAAT, taken at a Klinik Kesihatan for dysuria, is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. He returns for the result with ongoing mild urethral discharge. The referral laboratory can process gonococcal culture.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Treat now; culture adds nothing once NAAT is positive
Take a urethral culture and treat when sensitivities return
Take a urethral culture, then treat today without waiting
Repeat the NAAT on a urethral swab to confirm the result
Send serum gonococcal antibodies before treating him
mcq.e: NAAT is highly sensitive (> 95%) but gives **no antimicrobial susceptibility** data. Anyone diagnosed by NAAT should have **cultures taken from infected sites before treatment** to monitor resistance, but **treatment is given without waiting** for the result. Gonococcal culture must be specifically requested and reach the laboratory within 24 hours on selective media.
w: Wrong - Culture provides susceptibility testing and resistance surveillance that NAAT cannot.
Wrong - Delaying treatment prolongs infectivity and complications; do not wait for culture.
Correct - Culture infected sites before treatment for susceptibility, then treat the same day.
Wrong - A positive NAAT needs no confirmation before treatment, and NAAT gives no sensitivities.
Wrong - There is no useful serological test for gonorrhoea.

mcq.stem:
A 20-year-old female university student has an opportunistic self-collected vaginal swab at a Klinik Kesihatan. NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for gonorrhoea. She is asymptomatic, not pregnant and has no allergies.
What is the guideline's preferred treatment?
o: Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
Azithromycin 1g PO as a single stat dose
Amoxicillin 500mg PO 8-hourly for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM plus azithromycin 1g
Metronidazole 400mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
mcq.e: For uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal or pharyngeal chlamydia the preferred regimen is **doxycycline 100mg 12-hourly for 7 days**; **azithromycin 1g stat is the alternative** (doxycycline is more effective, especially for rectal infection). Amoxicillin is reserved for pregnancy. She should abstain until she and her partners have completed treatment, and partners from the last 60 days are treated.
w: Correct - Non-pregnant uncomplicated chlamydia: doxycycline 100mg 12-hourly for 7 days.
Wrong - Azithromycin 1g stat is the alternative, not the preferred regimen outside pregnancy.
Wrong - Amoxicillin is an alternative only in pregnancy.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone is unnecessary when gonorrhoea NAAT is negative.
Wrong - Metronidazole treats trichomonas and BV, not chlamydia.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks gestation has a positive chlamydia NAAT on a vulvovaginal swab taken at antenatal booking in a Klinik Kesihatan. She is asymptomatic and has no drug allergy.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
Ciprofloxacin 500mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
Metronidazole 400mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM as a single stat dose
Azithromycin 1g PO as a single stat dose
mcq.e: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, so chlamydia in pregnancy is treated with **azithromycin 1g stat** (alternative **amoxicillin 500mg 8-hourly for 7 days**). Untreated chlamydia in pregnancy is linked to preterm rupture of membranes, preterm birth, low birth weight and neonatal conjunctivitis or pneumonia. A **test of cure is recommended in pregnancy**, no earlier than 4 weeks after treatment.
w: Wrong - Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - Quinolones are avoided in pregnancy and are not chlamydia regimens here.
Wrong - Metronidazole does not treat chlamydia.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea, not chlamydia.
Correct - Chlamydia in pregnancy: azithromycin 1g stat (or amoxicillin for 7 days).

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation was treated with azithromycin 1g for genital chlamydia. Her husband was treated at the same time and she now has no symptoms.
When should her test of cure be done?
o: Not needed, as she is asymptomatic and he was treated
NAAT no earlier than 4 weeks after treatment
NAAT 7 days after completing her treatment
Chlamydia serology 6 weeks after treatment
Endocervical culture 14 days after treatment
mcq.e: Test of cure is **not routine** for uncomplicated chlamydia but **is recommended in pregnancy**, with suspected poor compliance and with persistent symptoms. It should be done by NAAT **no earlier than 4 weeks** after treatment, because non-viable chlamydial DNA can remain detectable for up to 4 weeks and give a false positive. Chlamydia serology is not recommended for diagnosis.
w: Wrong - Pregnancy is an indication for test of cure even when asymptomatic.
Correct - Pregnancy: test of cure by NAAT no earlier than 4 weeks after treatment.
Wrong - At 7 days residual non-viable DNA can give a false-positive NAAT.
Wrong - Chlamydia serology is not recommended for diagnosis or test of cure.
Wrong - Culture is not the recommended test; NAAT is used.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 10 days of mild dysuria and a scanty mucoid urethral discharge seen only on milking. Urethral Gram stain shows 8 polymorphs per high-power field and no Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Urine NAAT is negative for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline for 7 days
Ciprofloxacin 500mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
Metronidazole 2g PO as a single stat dose
Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
Moxifloxacin 400mg PO daily for 10-14 days
mcq.e: **5 or more polymorphs per high-power field** with no Gram-negative diplococci defines **non-gonococcal urethritis**, which has many causes besides chlamydia (Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma, T. vaginalis, adenovirus, HSV). A first episode is treated with **doxycycline 100mg 12-hourly for 7 days** (alternative: azithromycin 500mg then 250mg daily for 4 days). Partners from the preceding 60 days should be evaluated and given an anti-chlamydial regimen.
w: Wrong - Ceftriaxone is not needed when gonorrhoea has been excluded.
Wrong - Ciprofloxacin is not a recommended NGU regimen.
Wrong - Metronidazole is added only for recurrent or persistent NGU.
Correct - First episode of NGU: doxycycline 100mg 12-hourly for 7 days.
Wrong - Moxifloxacin is for recurrent NGU after first-line azithromycin.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old man completed doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days for non-gonococcal urethritis 5 weeks ago. His only partner was treated and there has been no other sexual contact. His urethral discharge has returned, and Gram stain again shows 10 polymorphs per high-power field without diplococci.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Repeat doxycycline 100mg BD for a further 7 days
Moxifloxacin 400mg daily for 10-14 days plus metronidazole
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus azithromycin 1g PO STAT
Azithromycin 500mg then 250mg for 4 days plus metronidazole
Doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days plus fluconazole 150mg
mcq.e: Recurrent or persistent NGU (with reinfection excluded) after **first-line doxycycline** is treated with **azithromycin 500mg stat then 250mg daily for 4 days plus metronidazole 400mg BD for 5 days**, covering Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas vaginalis. **Moxifloxacin plus metronidazole** is used if azithromycin was the first-line drug. Multiplex PCR helps identify the organism in recurrent cases.
w: Wrong - Repeating the same drug does not cover doxycycline-resistant organisms such as M. genitalium.
Wrong - Moxifloxacin plus metronidazole is for recurrence after first-line azithromycin.
Wrong - Gonorrhoea is unlikely with no diplococci and no new exposure.
Correct - Recurrence after doxycycline: extended azithromycin plus metronidazole 5 days.
Wrong - Prolonged doxycycline and antifungals are not guideline regimens for NGU.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of gradually increasing left scrotal pain and swelling, dysuria and urethral discharge. Temperature is 37.9°C. The left epididymis is swollen and tender, the testis lies normally and the cremasteric reflex is present. Urethral Gram stain shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 10-14 days alone
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline 100mg BD 10 days
Levofloxacin 500mg PO once daily for 10 days
Ceftriaxone 1g IM daily for 7 days plus azithromycin 1g PO
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 625mg PO 8-hourly for 7 days
mcq.e: Under 35 years, epididymo-orchitis is usually **sexually acquired** (C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae). With gonorrhoea likely, treat with **ceftriaxone 500mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100mg BD for 10 days**, with scrotal support and NSAIDs. Doxycycline alone for 10-14 days is used when the cause is STI-related but gonorrhoea is unlikely, and levofloxacin is for enteric organisms.
w: Wrong - Doxycycline alone is for STI-related cases where gonorrhoea is unlikely; diplococci are seen here.
Correct - STI-related epididymo-orchitis: ceftriaxone 500mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100mg BD for 10 days.
Wrong - Levofloxacin is for enteric organisms and misses resistant gonococci.
Wrong - This is not a guideline regimen, and azithromycin 1g is too short for epididymo-orchitis.
Wrong - Co-amoxiclav covers neither gonorrhoea reliably nor chlamydia.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with 2 days of right scrotal pain and swelling, fever, frequency and dysuria. He has been married for 35 years with no other sexual partners. The right epididymis is tender and swollen; urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
What is the most appropriate antibiotic?
o: Levofloxacin 500mg PO once daily for 10 days
Ceftriaxone 500mg IM STAT plus doxycycline for 10 days
Doxycycline 100mg PO 12-hourly for 10-14 days
Azithromycin 1g PO as a single stat dose
Nitrofurantoin 100mg PO 12-hourly for 7 days
mcq.e: Over 35 years and without STI risk, epididymo-orchitis is usually due to **enteric/urinary Gram-negative organisms** such as E. coli, often with an underlying anatomical or functional abnormality (here BPH) that should be investigated. Treat with **levofloxacin 500mg daily for 10 days** (or ofloxacin 200mg BD for 14 days) after sending an MSU for culture. Nitrofurantoin reaches the bladder but not the epididymis.
w: Correct - Enteric epididymo-orchitis in an older man: levofloxacin 500mg daily for 10 days.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline targets sexually acquired organisms, unlikely here.
Wrong - Doxycycline alone is for STI-related cases where gonorrhoea is unlikely.
Wrong - Single-dose azithromycin does not treat Gram-negative epididymal infection.
Wrong - Nitrofurantoin gives no useful tissue levels in the epididymis or testis.

mcq.stem:
A 15-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with sudden severe left testicular pain that woke him 3 hours ago, with vomiting. He denies sexual activity. The left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. Urine dipstick is normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start ceftriaxone and doxycycline; review in 3 days
Arrange an outpatient scrotal Doppler ultrasound this week
Give NSAIDs and scrotal support; review tomorrow
Send urine NAAT and MSU culture, then decide
Refer immediately to surgeons for exploration
mcq.e: Sudden severe pain, vomiting, a high-riding horizontal testis and an absent cremasteric reflex suggest **testicular torsion**, a surgical emergency that **must be considered and excluded first** in every acute scrotum. Testicular salvage falls sharply after about 6 hours, so the boy needs immediate surgical referral; imaging or tests must not delay exploration. Epididymo-orchitis is usually gradual in onset with urethritis or urinary symptoms.
w: Wrong - Treating as epididymo-orchitis delays surgery and risks losing the testis.
Wrong - An outpatient scan wastes the short window for testicular salvage.
Wrong - Analgesia and review tomorrow is unsafe in suspected torsion.
Wrong - Waiting for urine results delays the emergency.
Correct - Suspected torsion: immediate surgical referral for exploration.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man with sexually acquired epididymo-orchitis was started on ceftriaxone 500mg IM and doxycycline 100mg BD at a Klinik Kesihatan. Three days later his pain and swelling are no better, although he is taking the tablets and is afebrile.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue treatment and review at 2 weeks as planned
Add levofloxacin 500mg daily to cover enteric organisms
Reassess diagnosis: scrotal ultrasound or surgical review
Extend the doxycycline course to a total of 21 days instead
Give a second dose of ceftriaxone 500mg IM today
mcq.e: The guideline says that if there is **no clinical improvement after 3 days, the diagnosis should be reviewed**. Consider abscess, testicular infarction, torsion, tumour, or other infections such as TB or mumps, using ultrasound and surgical review. Routine review is at 2 weeks for compliance, partner notification and resolution, watching for hydrocoele, abscess, infarction and infertility.
w: Wrong - No improvement at 3 days is a trigger to review the diagnosis, not to wait.
Wrong - Adding antibiotics without reassessment may miss abscess, infarction or tumour.
Correct - No improvement after 3 days: review the diagnosis with ultrasound or surgical review.
Wrong - Lengthening treatment does not address a possibly wrong diagnosis.
Wrong - A repeat ceftriaxone dose does not address abscess, infarction or another cause.

mcq.stem:
A 3-day-old baby boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with bilateral, thick, profuse yellow eye discharge and markedly swollen eyelids. He was born vaginally at home; the mother had no antenatal care. A fresh eye swab Gram stain shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci. He has no fever and is feeding well.
Which treatment should be arranged, together with urgent referral?
o: Ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg (max 250 mg) IV/IM as a single dose
Chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops two-hourly for 7 days alone
Erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day orally in 4 divided doses for 14 days
Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 2 weeks
Azithromycin 20 mg/kg orally once daily for 3 days
mcq.e: Onset at 2–5 days with hyperpurulent discharge and gram-negative intracellular diplococci on Gram stain indicates gonococcal ophthalmia, which can perforate the cornea within days. Systemic ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg (max 250 mg) IV/IM stat is preferred, with hourly saline irrigation and ophthalmology referral; topical antibiotics are optional. Gonococcal ophthalmia is notifiable.
w: Correct - Gonococcal ophthalmia needs systemic ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg (max 250 mg) stat; cefotaxime 100 mg/kg is the alternative.
Wrong - Topical antibiotics are optional adjuncts only; topical treatment alone will not prevent corneal perforation.
Wrong - Erythromycin for 14 days is the regimen for chlamydial ophthalmia, which presents later (5–14 days).
Wrong - IV acyclovir treats herpes simplex conjunctivitis, which presents with vesicles rather than gram-negative diplococci.
Wrong - Azithromycin 20 mg/kg for 3 days is the alternative for chlamydial, not gonococcal, ophthalmia.

mcq.stem:
A 10-day-old girl has had a sticky left eye for 3 days that has become purulent, with mild lid swelling. She is otherwise well. The mother had untreated vaginal discharge in the third trimester. Gram stain shows pus cells but no gram-negative diplococci; an eye-swab NAAT is sent and the ophthalmologist confirms there is no keratitis.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Chloramphenicol eye drops and saline irrigation for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IM as a single stat dose only
Erythromycin 0.5% eye ointment to both eyes four times daily for 14 days
Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days
Watchful waiting with saline cleaning until NAAT returns
mcq.e: Onset at 5–14 days with no diplococci points to Chlamydia trachomatis, the commonest cause of ophthalmia neonatorum. Systemic treatment is essential because the infant may also carry nasopharyngeal infection and later develop pneumonia; local treatment may be unnecessary if systemic treatment is given. Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days is preferred (azithromycin 20 mg/kg daily for 3 days is the alternative); warn parents about pyloric stenosis with both drugs.
w: Wrong - Topical antibiotics alone do not clear chlamydial infection or prevent chlamydial pneumonia.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone is for gonococcal ophthalmia, which typically presents earlier at 2–5 days.
Wrong - Topical erythromycin is not adequate; systemic treatment is essential in chlamydial ophthalmia.
Correct - Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days treats the eye and systemic infection.
Wrong - Ophthalmia neonatorum is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should not be delayed for results.

mcq.stem:
A 9-day-old baby is reviewed at a Klinik Kesihatan for a red, watery right eye. There are clustered vesicles on the right upper eyelid and the cornea appears hazy. The mother recalls painful genital sores in late pregnancy. The baby is afebrile and feeding normally.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Topical acyclovir ointment and review at the clinic in 48 hours
Admit for IV acyclovir, lumbar puncture and ophthalmology review
Oral erythromycin for 14 days and refer parents to an STI clinic
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone and hourly saline eye irrigation
Swab the vesicles for HSV NAAT and treat only if it is positive
mcq.e: Vesicles around the eye with corneal involvement suggest neonatal herpes simplex infection, which may be generalised (skin, eye, mucosa) even when the baby looks well. The guideline requires lumbar puncture and ophthalmology assessment, with IV acyclovir for 2 weeks. A swab for HSV NAAT is taken, but treatment is not delayed for the result.
w: Wrong - Topical therapy is inadequate for neonatal HSV; it can disseminate to the CNS and needs IV acyclovir.
Correct - Periocular vesicles with corneal involvement need admission, IV acyclovir, LP and ophthalmology review.
Wrong - Erythromycin treats chlamydial ophthalmia; it has no activity against herpes simplex virus.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone is for gonococcal ophthalmia and does not treat a viral infection.
Wrong - Swabs are taken, but delaying IV therapy for results risks disseminated or CNS disease.

mcq.stem:
A 6-day-old boy has just been treated in hospital for conjunctivitis with a positive Neisseria gonorrhoeae NAAT on his eye swab. His 19-year-old mother is asymptomatic and attends with him at the Klinik Kesihatan; her own tests have not been done.
Which action for the family is most appropriate?
o: Test the mother first and treat her only if her own NAAT result is positive
Reassure the parents, as the baby has now been fully treated and cured
Screen only the mother, as the father has no genital symptoms
Advise the mother to avoid breastfeeding until she is retested
Treat the mother epidemiologically and refer both parents to STI clinic
