mcq.e: Ophthalmia neonatorum is a marker of maternal genital infection. The mother should be treated on epidemiological grounds without waiting for results, and both parents referred to an STI clinic for screening (particularly C. trachomatis, HSV and HIV). RPR of infant and mother is checked to exclude congenital syphilis, the case is notified, and the baby is reviewed at 2 weeks with a repeat eye swab.
w: Wrong - The mother is treated on epidemiological grounds; waiting for her result risks reinfection and missed treatment.
Wrong - Curing the baby does not treat the mother or her partner, who remain infected.
Wrong - Male gonococcal infection may be asymptomatic; both parents should be referred for screening.
Wrong - Gonorrhoea is not a reason to stop breastfeeding; the issue is treating the parents.
Correct - The mother is treated epidemiologically and both parents are referred for STI screening.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old woman with a new partner presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 4 days of bilateral lower abdominal pain and deep dyspareunia. Temperature is 37.6°C and she is haemodynamically stable. There is cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness, with no peritonism. Urine pregnancy test is negative. Endocervical swabs have been taken.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to confirm PID before any antibiotics
Wait for the swab results and treat according to the organism found
Start empirical outpatient antibiotics today and review in 72 hours
Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy to confirm the diagnosis first
Give a single dose of azithromycin and review the swab results
mcq.e: Clinical signs of PID have low sensitivity and specificity, but untreated PID risks infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain. Therefore empirical treatment should start immediately on suspicion, after swabs and a pregnancy test, with review at 72 hours. Ultrasound is of limited value in uncomplicated PID and is reserved for suspected abscess or hydrosalpinx.
w: Wrong - Ultrasound is of limited value in uncomplicated PID; it is used when an abscess or hydrosalpinx is suspected.
Wrong - Delaying treatment for results increases long-term sequelae such as infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
Correct - Mild–moderate PID is treated empirically as an outpatient at once, with review at 72 hours.
Wrong - Laparoscopy is not needed to start treatment and is reserved for selected or severe cases.
Wrong - A single dose of azithromycin does not cover gonorrhoea or anaerobes and is not a PID regimen.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old woman is diagnosed with mild pelvic inflammatory disease at a Klinik Kesihatan. She is afebrile, tolerating oral intake and has no drug allergies. Pregnancy test is negative.
Which regimen is the preferred outpatient treatment?
o: Cefixime 400 mg PO stat, doxycycline 100 mg q12h and metronidazole 400 mg q12h for 14 days
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 7 days
Azithromycin 1 g PO stat plus metronidazole 400 mg PO q12h for 7 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 625 mg PO q8h plus doxycycline 100 mg q12h for 14 days
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat, doxycycline 100 mg q12h and metronidazole 400 mg q12h for 14 days
mcq.e: The preferred outpatient regimen covers gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone 500 mg IM), chlamydia (doxycycline) and anaerobes (metronidazole), with the oral drugs given for 14 days. The guideline specifically says IM ceftriaxone must not be replaced by an oral cephalosporin such as cefixime, as there is no trial evidence and tissue levels are likely to be lower.
w: Wrong - Oral cefixime must not replace IM ceftriaxone in PID, as there is no supporting trial evidence.
Wrong - This lacks anaerobic cover, uses the wrong ceftriaxone dose and is too short; PID needs 14 days.
Wrong - This lacks reliable gonococcal cover and is too short for upper genital tract infection.
Wrong - Co-amoxiclav plus doxycycline is not a guideline PID regimen and gives poor gonococcal cover.
Correct - Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat plus 14 days of doxycycline and metronidazole is preferred.

mcq.stem:
Five women are diagnosed with PID at a Klinik Kesihatan. All are haemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake and have no signs of peritonitis.
Which patient should be admitted for inpatient treatment?
o: A 27-year-old with an intrauterine pregnancy of 8 weeks on scan
A 17-year-old with her first episode and a temperature of 37.8°C
A 30-year-old with a copper IUD inserted two years ago
A 24-year-old with chlamydia treated six months ago
A 35-year-old with a negative endocervical swab NAAT result
mcq.e: Admission (preferably under gynaecology) is indicated when a surgical emergency cannot be excluded, there is no response to or intolerance of oral therapy, severe disease (temperature above 38°C, peritonitis), a tubo-ovarian abscess, or PID in pregnancy. Pregnancy raises maternal and foetal morbidity, so parenteral therapy is advised. Young age, an IUD, past chlamydia or a negative swab are not admission criteria.
w: Correct - PID in pregnancy is an admission criterion, as parenteral therapy is advised.
Wrong - Fever above 38°C indicates severe disease; 37.8°C alone in a stable teenager does not mandate admission.
Wrong - An IUD alone is not an indication for admission; mild PID with an IUD is treated as an outpatient.
Wrong - Past chlamydia is a risk factor but not an admission criterion.
Wrong - Pathogen-negative PID is common and does not alter the treatment setting.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman with a copper IUD inserted 18 months ago is diagnosed with mild PID at a Klinik Kesihatan. She had unprotected intercourse 3 days ago and does not want to become pregnant. She asks whether the coil must come out.
What is the most appropriate management of the IUD?
o: Remove the IUD today before starting the first antibiotic dose
Leave it in, treat, and consider removal if no response in 48–72 hours
Remove the IUD after completing the 14-day antibiotic course in all cases
Remove the IUD today and insert a new one once the infection is cured
Leave it in situ but halve the antibiotic course to 7 days
mcq.e: Removal of an IUD in suspected PID must be balanced against the risk of pregnancy if there was unprotected intercourse in the preceding 7 days. The IUD can stay while antibiotics are given, with removal considered if there is no response within 48–72 hours; hormonal emergency contraception may be appropriate if it is removed. The 14-day course is unchanged.
w: Wrong - Immediate removal after intercourse 3 days ago risks pregnancy and is not mandatory.
Correct - Keep the IUD, start treatment and consider removal if there is no response within 48–72 hours.
Wrong - Routine removal after successful treatment is not required.
Wrong - Immediate removal is not required and exposes her to pregnancy from recent intercourse.
Wrong - The IUD does not change the duration; PID is treated for 14 days.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old married woman has mild PID. She had an anaphylactic reaction to ceftriaxone last year. She has been with one partner for 8 years and both have a low risk of gonorrhoea. She is not pregnant.
Which outpatient regimen is most appropriate?
o: Cefixime 400 mg PO stat plus doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 14 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO stat plus metronidazole 400 mg PO q12h for 7 days
Clindamycin 300 mg PO q12h for 7 days as monotherapy
Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO q24h for 14 days
Azithromycin 1 g PO stat plus doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 7 days
mcq.e: For cephalosporin allergy with low gonorrhoea risk, the alternatives are levofloxacin 500 mg daily plus metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days, or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily alone for 14 days (it has anaerobic activity). Quinolone resistance limits their use when gonorrhoea is likely. An oral cephalosporin is unsuitable both because of the allergy and because it should never replace IM ceftriaxone.
w: Wrong - Cefixime is a cephalosporin (allergy) and oral cephalosporins should not replace IM ceftriaxone.
Wrong - A single dose of ciprofloxacin with 7 days of metronidazole is not a PID regimen; PID needs 14 days.
Wrong - Oral clindamycin alone for 7 days does not cover chlamydia adequately and is too short.
Correct - Moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 14 days is the guideline alternative for low gonorrhoea risk.
Wrong - This lacks anaerobic cover and is shorter than the 14 days required for PID.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old woman starts outpatient treatment for PID. Her endocervical gonorrhoea culture and chlamydia NAAT are both negative. She has had one male partner for the past 4 months, who is asymptomatic.
What is the most appropriate advice about her partner?
o: No partner treatment is needed because her swabs were negative
Treat the partner only if his own urine NAAT is positive
Treat him for chlamydia and gonorrhoea irrespective of test results
Treat the partner with metronidazole alone for anaerobic cover
Examine him and treat only if a urethral discharge is seen on examination
mcq.e: Partners from the last 60 days must be treated epidemiologically for chlamydia and gonorrhoea irrespective of test results, because pathogen-negative PID is common (the cervical infection may have cleared or tests may miss it) and an untreated partner causes reinfection. Both should avoid intercourse until they have completed treatment and follow-up.
w: Wrong - Negative swabs do not exclude a sexually acquired cause; pathogen-negative PID is common.
Wrong - Partner treatment is epidemiological and should not wait for his test result.
Correct - Partners within the last 60 days are treated for chlamydia and gonorrhoea regardless of results.
Wrong - Partner treatment targets chlamydia and gonorrhoea; metronidazole alone does not cover them.
Wrong - Male urethral infection is often asymptomatic, so treatment should not depend on signs.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan with a 2-week history of a thin, watery, greyish-white vaginal discharge with a fishy smell that is worse after intercourse. She has no itch or dysuria. Speculum shows a homogeneous discharge coating the vaginal walls with no vulval or vaginal redness and a normal cervix. Vaginal pH is 5.5 and a fishy odour is released on adding 10% KOH.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Trichomonas vaginalis infection
Bacterial vaginosis
Vulvovaginal candidiasis
Chlamydial mucopurulent cervicitis
Atrophic (oestrogen-deficient) vaginitis
mcq.e: She meets Amsel's criteria (3 of 4 needed): thin homogeneous discharge, pH above 4.5 and a positive whiff test; clue cells on wet mount would complete the set. BV is the commonest cause of vaginal discharge in reproductive-age women and characteristically causes no inflammation. Trichomoniasis can also raise pH and smell, but usually causes vulvovaginitis and a frothy yellow discharge.
w: Wrong - Trichomoniasis usually gives a frothy yellow discharge with vulvitis and sometimes a strawberry cervix.
Correct - Thin homogeneous discharge, pH above 4.5 and a positive whiff test meet Amsel's criteria.
Wrong - Candidiasis causes itch and a thick curdy discharge with a normal pH (4.5 or below).
Wrong - Cervicitis gives mucopurulent cervical discharge and contact bleeding, not a fishy vaginal discharge.
Wrong - Atrophic vaginitis occurs after menopause with thin, pale, inflamed mucosa.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old married woman (not pregnant) has symptomatic vaginal discharge. Wet mount shows clue cells, vaginal pH is 5.0 and the whiff test is positive. She has one long-term partner who is asymptomatic. She asks whether her husband needs treatment and whether she must return for a repeat swab.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Metronidazole 2 g stat for both partners, then a test of cure in 4 weeks’ time
Metronidazole for her and her husband together, with no test of cure
Clindamycin 300 mg q12h for 7 days for her and a test of cure in 2 weeks
Metronidazole 400 mg q12h for 5–7 days for her only, with no test of cure
Fluconazole 150 mg stat for her and a urine NAAT for her husband
mcq.e: Bacterial vaginosis is an imbalance of vaginal flora, not an STI requiring partner management: routine screening and treatment of male partners is not indicated, and tests of cure are not needed. Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5–7 days is preferred (2 g stat and clindamycin are alternatives). Relapse is common (30% at one month), so advise avoiding douching and antiseptic washes.
w: Wrong - Partner treatment and test of cure are both not indicated in BV.
Wrong - Treating male partners does not reduce BV recurrence and is not recommended.
Wrong - Clindamycin is only the alternative, and a test of cure is not indicated.
Correct - Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5–7 days for her alone; no partner treatment or test of cure.
Wrong - Fluconazole treats candidiasis; partner NAAT is not part of BV management.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old woman has a routine cervical smear at a Klinik Kesihatan. She has no vaginal discharge, odour or itch and is not pregnant. The cytology report mentions clue cells and a shift in flora suggestive of Gardnerella. She asks whether she needs medicine.
What is the most appropriate response?
o: No treatment, as she has no symptoms and is not pregnant
Metronidazole 400 mg q12h for 7 days to prevent PID
Metronidazole 2 g stat for her and her husband today
Clindamycin 300 mg q12h for 7 days, then repeat the smear in 3 months
Clotrimazole 500 mg pessary stat, then a repeat swab
mcq.e: Around half of women with BV are asymptomatic, and the guideline indicates treatment for women with BV who have symptoms. Spontaneous resolution is common. The exception is pregnancy in women at higher risk of preterm birth, who may benefit from screening and treatment.
w: Correct - Treatment is indicated for symptomatic BV; an incidental finding in a non-pregnant woman needs none.
Wrong - Asymptomatic BV in a non-pregnant woman does not need treatment.
Wrong - Neither treatment nor partner treatment is indicated here.
Wrong - She needs no treatment and a repeat smear for BV is not required.
Wrong - Clotrimazole treats candidiasis, not bacterial vaginosis.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation attends a Klinik Kesihatan with vulval itch and a profuse frothy yellow-green offensive discharge. Speculum shows punctate haemorrhages on the cervix. A saline wet mount from the posterior fornix shows motile flagellated organisms.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Metronidazole 2 g PO stat for her alone, as it improves adherence
Defer treatment until after 16 weeks to avoid first-trimester exposure
Clotrimazole 500 mg pessary stat and review her in one week
Clindamycin 300 mg PO q12h for 7 days, as metronidazole is unsafe
Metronidazole 400 mg PO q12h for 7 days with her partner treated too
mcq.e: Motile flagellates with a frothy discharge and strawberry cervix indicate Trichomonas vaginalis. Metronidazole can be used at all stages of pregnancy and in breastfeeding, but single high-dose (2 g) regimens are not recommended in pregnancy, so the 7-day course is used. Partners must be treated simultaneously, avoiding sex (including oral sex) for at least a week and until both complete treatment.
w: Wrong - Single 2 g doses are not recommended in pregnancy, and fail more often if partners are untreated.
Wrong - Metronidazole is not teratogenic and can be used in all trimesters; treatment should not be delayed.
Wrong - Clotrimazole treats candidiasis and has no role against Trichomonas.
Wrong - Metronidazole is safe in pregnancy; clindamycin is not a trichomoniasis regimen.
Correct - Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days, with simultaneous partner treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan because his wife was diagnosed with Trichomonas vaginalis yesterday. He has no urethral discharge or dysuria and his examination is normal. He is started on metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days.
Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Resume sex once his own urine NAAT comes back negative
Avoid sex for 48 hours after taking the first metronidazole dose
Avoid all sex, including oral sex, for 1 week and until both finish
Avoid vaginal sex only, as oral sex does not transmit Trichomonas
Return for a test-of-cure NAAT two weeks after his treatment course ends
mcq.e: Infection in men is often asymptomatic (15–50%), so male partners are treated simultaneously without waiting for tests. Both should avoid sex, including oral sex, for at least 1 week and until both have completed treatment. A test of cure is only needed if symptoms persist or recur.
w: Wrong - He is treated epidemiologically; a negative NAAT does not shorten abstinence.
Wrong - Abstinence should last at least 1 week and until both have completed treatment.
Correct - Avoid all sex, including oral sex, for 1 week and until both have completed treatment.
Wrong - The guideline advice specifically includes oral sex in the abstinence period.
Wrong - Test of cure is only recommended if symptoms persist or recur after treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with intense vulval itch and a thick, white, curd-like discharge. The vulva is erythematous with satellite pustules. Vaginal pH is 4.2. She has had no previous episodes this year.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Fluconazole 150 mg PO as a single stat dose
Clotrimazole 500 mg vaginal pessary as a single dose
Fluconazole 150 mg PO every 72 hours for three doses
Metronidazole 400 mg PO q12h for 7 days
Oral nystatin for 14 days to clear gut colonisation
mcq.e: This is vulvovaginal candidiasis (itch, curdy discharge, normal pH). Oral azoles are contraindicated in pregnancy because of conflicting safety data, so topical treatment is used: clotrimazole 500 mg vaginal pessary stat, and pregnant women may need a longer topical course of at least 7 days. Topical azole to the vulva and 1% hydrocortisone can relieve symptoms.
w: Wrong - Fluconazole and other oral azoles are best avoided in pregnancy.
Correct - Topical clotrimazole is the choice in pregnancy; a longer topical course may be needed.
Wrong - Repeated oral fluconazole is for complicated infection and is avoided in pregnancy.
Wrong - Metronidazole treats BV or trichomoniasis, not candidiasis.
Wrong - There is no evidence that treating gut colonisation helps; topical azole is required.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old woman has had five culture-confirmed episodes of vulvovaginal candidiasis in the past 12 months, each responding to a single clotrimazole pessary. She is not pregnant. HbA1c and HIV tests are normal, and she takes no steroids or antibiotics.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Fluconazole 150–200 mg q72h for 3 doses, then weekly for 6 months
Fluconazole 150 mg stat for her and for her asymptomatic husband
Clotrimazole 500 mg pessary stat at the start of each new episode
Daily oral probiotic and a low-sugar diet to prevent recurrence
Itraconazole 200 mg PO daily for 6 months with liver monitoring
mcq.e: Recurrent VVC is 4 or more episodes in 12 months, confirmed by culture at least once, after checking for diabetes, HIV, steroids and antibiotic use. Treatment is induction with fluconazole 150–200 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses, then weekly for 6 months (alternative: weekly clotrimazole 500 mg pessary for 6 months). Partner treatment, diet and probiotics have no proven effect, and no hepatic monitoring is needed at these doses.
w: Correct - Induction then weekly fluconazole for 6 months is the regimen for recurrent infection.
Wrong - Contact tracing is not required and asymptomatic male partners need no treatment.
Wrong - Episodic single doses treat each attack but do not suppress recurrent infection.
Wrong - There is no evidence that diet or probiotics reduce recurrence.
Wrong - Daily itraconazole is not the guideline regimen, and fluconazole needs no liver monitoring.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman has vulval itch and soreness with superficial dyspareunia for one week. The vulva is erythematous and excoriated, but there is little discharge. Vaginal pH is 4.0. A Gram stain of vaginal secretions shows no yeast cells or pseudohyphae and no clue cells.
What is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: HSV NAAT swab from the excoriated vulval skin
Type-specific HSV serology for HSV-1 and HSV-2
Vulval biopsy to exclude lichen sclerosus
High vaginal swab for Candida culture
Trichomonas NAAT from a vulvovaginal swab
mcq.e: Vulvovaginal candidiasis can occur with normal or absent discharge, and microscopy (Gram stain or 10% KOH) misses some cases. The guideline recommends culture for symptomatic women with negative microscopy. Culture also identifies non-albicans species, such as C. glabrata, which may respond poorly to standard azoles.
w: Wrong - She has no vesicles or ulcers, so HSV NAAT is not the next test.
Wrong - Type-specific HSV serology is not used to diagnose an acute vulvitis.
Wrong - Biopsy is premature after one week of symptoms suggesting candidiasis.
Correct - Culture is indicated in symptomatic women with negative microscopy.
Wrong - Trichomonas causes discharge, raised pH and odour; the picture favours candidiasis.

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old woman presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of painful genital sores, dysuria, fever and myalgia. She has never had similar lesions. There are multiple bilateral shallow ulcers and vesicles on the labia with tender bilateral inguinal nodes. New vesicles are still appearing.
What is the most appropriate management today?
o: Acyclovir 5% cream five times daily for 5 days
Swab for HSV NAAT and start antiviral treatment only once it is positive
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7–10 days with supportive care
Acyclovir 800 mg PO q8h for 2 days with salt-water baths
Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM stat and RPR testing
mcq.e: A first episode with systemic symptoms and bilateral ulcers should be treated on clinical suspicion with oral acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 7–10 days, given within 5 days of onset or while new lesions form. Topical agents are less effective and promote resistance. Supportive measures include saline bathing, analgesia, topical lidocaine and passing urine in water.
w: Wrong - Topical antivirals are not recommended, as they are less effective and generate resistance.
Wrong - Therapy should start on clinical suspicion; waiting for results lets the episode progress.
Correct - A first episode is treated with acyclovir 400 mg q8h for 7–10 days on clinical suspicion.
Wrong - The 2-day high-dose course is an episodic regimen for recurrences, not a first episode.
Wrong - Syphilis serology should be done, but painful multiple vesicles indicate herpes, not syphilis.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man with confirmed genital HSV-2 has had 8 recurrences in the past year, each lasting about a week. They cause him considerable distress and affect his relationship. He is otherwise well with normal renal function.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Acyclovir 800 mg PO q8h for 2 days at the start of each recurrence
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7–10 days with each recurrence
Topical acyclovir cream applied at the first sign of each recurrence
Supportive care only, as recurrences are self-limiting and mild
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q12h continuously for up to 1 year, then reassess
mcq.e: Suppressive therapy is indicated with 6 or more recurrences a year (or severe, prolonged or psychologically distressing episodes): acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for up to 1 year, then reassess. It cuts recurrences by 70–80% and improves quality of life but does not eliminate subclinical shedding, so condom advice still applies. Breakthrough recurrences can be managed by increasing to 400 mg three times daily.
w: Wrong - Episodic short courses suit infrequent recurrences; he qualifies for suppression.
Wrong - This is the first-episode regimen and does not prevent recurrences.
Wrong - Topical antivirals are not recommended for genital herpes.
Wrong - With 8 recurrences a year and distress, suppressive therapy is clearly indicated.
Correct - At 6 or more recurrences a year, give acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for up to 1 year.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks' gestation presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with painful vesicles and shallow ulcers on both labia, dysuria and malaise. She has never had genital sores before. Her obstetric course has otherwise been normal.
What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Acyclovir 400 mg q8h for 7–10 days and anticipate a vaginal delivery
Defer antivirals until after delivery to avoid foetal drug exposure
Type-specific HSV serology first, and decide delivery mode on the result
Acyclovir 400 mg q8h until delivery and plan a caesarean section
Supportive care now, then suppressive acyclovir from 36 weeks
mcq.e: A first episode acquired from 28 weeks carries the highest neonatal risk, because shedding may persist at delivery and maternal antibodies have not yet crossed to the baby (transmission about 41% with vaginal birth). Treatment should not be delayed: acyclovir 400 mg three times daily continued until delivery, with caesarean section recommended. Because up to 15% of apparent first episodes are recurrences, the plan assumes all first-episode lesions are primary.
w: Wrong - Vaginal delivery is anticipated for first or second trimester acquisition, not from 28 weeks.
Wrong - Acyclovir is considered safe in pregnancy and treatment should not be delayed.
Wrong - Delivery planning should assume a first episode is primary rather than wait for serology.
Correct - Third-trimester first episode: acyclovir until delivery and caesarean section.
Wrong - Suppression from 36 weeks is for recurrent herpes; a primary episode needs treatment now.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation has had recurrent genital herpes for 6 years, with 2–3 short recurrences a year. She has no lesions today. She is anxious about infecting her baby and asks about delivery.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Offer acyclovir 400 mg q8h from 36 weeks and anticipate vaginal delivery
Book an elective caesarean section at 38 weeks to protect the baby
No antiviral now; plan caesarean only if lesions appear in labour
Arrange IV acyclovir prophylaxis for the baby for 14 days after birth
Start acyclovir 400 mg q12h now and continue it for one year after delivery
mcq.e: With recurrent herpes, maternal IgG protects the baby and the neonatal risk is low (0–3% even if lesions are present at vaginal delivery). Vaginal delivery is anticipated, and suppressive acyclovir 400 mg three times daily from 36 weeks reduces shedding and recurrences at term, so fewer caesareans are needed. The baby needs only conservative care with advice to watch for lesions.
w: Correct - Suppressive acyclovir from 36 weeks with planned vaginal delivery is recommended.
Wrong - Recurrent herpes is not an indication for caesarean, as the neonatal risk is low.
Wrong - Even recurrent lesions in labour carry a low risk, and vaginal delivery should be offered.
Wrong - Babies of mothers with recurrent herpes need conservative care, not active treatment.
Wrong - The pregnancy regimen starts at 36 weeks at 400 mg three times daily until delivery.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old woman with a first episode of genital herpes, started on oral acyclovir 2 days ago, returns to a Klinik Kesihatan unable to pass urine for 14 hours. She has extensive vulval ulceration, a temperature of 37.9°C and a tender, palpable bladder. There is no neck stiffness.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Insert a urethral catheter in clinic and continue oral acyclovir
Switch to topical acyclovir and lidocaine gel, and review in 2 days
Give oral bethanechol and ask her to try voiding in a warm bath
Start oral amoxicillin for a presumed urinary tract infection
Refer for admission, using a suprapubic catheter if one is needed
mcq.e: Urinary retention in first-episode herpes is due to autonomic neuropathy or painful lesions, and is an indication for hospital admission. If catheterisation is needed the suprapubic route may be considered, to avoid the theoretical risk of ascending infection, reduce pain and allow trial voiding without repeated recatheterisation. Aseptic meningitis and severe constitutional symptoms are other reasons to admit.
w: Wrong - A urethral catheter through herpetic lesions is painful; the suprapubic route is preferred.
Wrong - Topical antivirals are ineffective and retention needs immediate relief.
Wrong - Voiding in water helps dysuria, but established retention with a palpable bladder needs admission.
Wrong - Retention here is due to herpes neuropathy or pain, not a bacterial UTI.
Correct - Urinary retention warrants admission, with suprapubic catheterisation if required.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a single, shallow, tender erosion on the penile shaft for 3 days, without vesicles. He has had several recent partners. The appearance is atypical and the doctor wants to confirm or exclude herpes simplex.
Which investigation is most appropriate?
o: Tzanck smear of ulcer-base scrapings for giant cells
HSV NAAT on a swab taken from the erosion
Type-specific HSV-1 and HSV-2 IgG serology
Viral culture of a swab, as it is the most sensitive test
Repeat type-specific serology in 2 weeks for a rise
mcq.e: HSV NAAT on a lesion swab is the test of choice: it detects type-specific DNA, has sensitivity and specificity above 90% and increases detection by 11–71% over culture. Culture is highly specific but insensitive, and the Tzanck smear is insensitive and nonspecific. Type-specific antibodies take 8–12 weeks to appear, so serology cannot diagnose a new lesion.
w: Wrong - The Tzanck smear is insensitive and nonspecific and should not be relied on.
Correct - NAAT from the lesion is the most sensitive and specific test, useful at all stages.
Wrong - Type-specific antibodies take 8–12 weeks to develop and do not diagnose the current lesion.
Wrong - Culture has low sensitivity, though specificity is virtually 100%.
Wrong - Seroconversion takes 8–12 weeks, so repeat serology at 2 weeks is unhelpful.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with multiple soft, cauliflower-like papules on the labia majora and perineum that have enlarged during pregnancy. They itch and occasionally bleed. She would like them treated.
Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Podophyllin 25% resin applied weekly by a nurse
Imiquimod 5% cream three times a week at bedtime
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen at the clinic
Podofilox 0.5% gel twice daily for 3 days a week
Sinecatechins 15% ointment applied three times daily
mcq.e: Podofilox, podophyllin and sinecatechins must not be used in pregnancy, and imiquimod should be avoided until more data are available. Provider-administered ablation (cryotherapy, TCA or surgical removal) is therefore used. Warts often proliferate and become friable in pregnancy and may not resolve fully until after delivery.
w: Wrong - Podophyllin is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - Imiquimod should be avoided in pregnancy until more data are available.
Correct - Cryotherapy is a provider-administered treatment that is safe in pregnancy.
Wrong - Podofilox is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - Sinecatechins should not be used during pregnancy.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man has had perianal warts treated with weekly cryotherapy at a Klinik Kesihatan for 4 months. Most have cleared, but one lesion has grown, become pigmented and feels firm and fixed. He is HIV-negative.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Take a biopsy of the lesion for histology
HPV DNA typing of a swab from the lesion
Continue cryotherapy for a further 3 months
Switch to imiquimod 5% cream for 16 weeks
Reassure him and review at the next visit
mcq.e: Diagnosis of warts is usually visual, but biopsy is indicated for atypical lesions (pigmented, indurated, fixed or ulcerated), diagnostic uncertainty, lesions not responding to standard therapy and to exclude malignancy. Most warts respond within 3 months. HPV testing is not recommended, as results are not confirmatory and do not guide management.
w: Correct - An atypical, non-responding lesion needs biopsy to exclude malignancy.
Wrong - HPV testing is not recommended, as it neither confirms nor guides wart management.
Wrong - Continuing ablation risks missing an intraepithelial neoplasia or carcinoma.
Wrong - Changing therapy without histology risks delaying a cancer diagnosis.
Wrong - A pigmented, firm, fixed lesion needs tissue diagnosis now.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old non-pregnant woman is found on speculum examination to have several small exophytic warts on the vaginal walls. The cervix looks normal and her cervical smear is up to date and normal. She has no external warts.
Which treatment is most appropriate for the vaginal warts?
o: Imiquimod 5% cream inserted into the vagina at bedtime
Podofilox 0.5% gel applied by the patient twice daily
Cryotherapy using a cryoprobe applied to the vaginal wall
Sinecatechins 15% ointment applied by the patient
Trichloroacetic acid 80–90% applied weekly by a clinician
mcq.e: Patient-applied treatments (imiquimod, podofilox, sinecatechins) are for external anogenital warts only. Vaginal, cervical and intra-anal warts are treated by the provider with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy, surgical removal or TCA/BCA. A cryoprobe must not be used in the vagina because of the risk of perforation and fistula.
w: Wrong - Imiquimod is a patient-applied treatment for external warts only.
Wrong - Podofilox is only for external anogenital warts.
Wrong - A cryoprobe in the vagina risks perforation and fistula; liquid nitrogen is used instead.
Wrong - Sinecatechins are only for external warts.
Correct - Provider-applied TCA or BCA weekly is a recommended option for vaginal warts.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man presents to a Klinik Kesihatan 6 days after paying for sex abroad. He has three painful, soft, non-indurated ulcers near the frenulum with ragged undermined edges and a purulent base that bleeds on contact. There is a painful fluctuant left inguinal node. RPR and HSV PCR from the ulcer are negative.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM stat and incision of the node at its base
Azithromycin 1 g PO stat and needle aspiration of the node via healthy skin
Doxycycline 100 mg q12h for 21 days and incision of the node
Acyclovir 400 mg q8h for 7–10 days and warm compresses to the node
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat and observation until the node bursts
mcq.e: Multiple painful, soft, undermined ulcers with a suppurative painful bubo, after syphilis and HSV are excluded, meet the criteria for probable chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi). Azithromycin 1 g stat is preferred (ceftriaxone 250 mg IM, ciprofloxacin or erythromycin are alternatives). Fluctuant buboes are aspirated with a needle through adjacent healthy skin, from the top not the base, which is simpler and safer than incision. Contacts in the 10 days before symptom onset are treated, and chancroid is notifiable.
w: Wrong - Penicillin does not treat H. ducreyi, and buboes are aspirated from the top, not cut at the base.
Correct - Azithromycin 1 g stat with needle aspiration of the bubo via healthy skin.
Wrong - A 21-day doxycycline course is for LGV, and chancroid is not treated this way.
Wrong - HSV PCR is negative, and herpes does not cause a suppurative bubo.
Wrong - Ceftriaxone is an alternative, but buboes should be aspirated rather than left to rupture.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man who has sex with men and is living with HIV presents with 2 weeks of severe anorectal pain, tenesmus, constipation and bloody mucopurulent rectal discharge. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Proctoscopy shows haemorrhagic proctitis with ulceration. Rectal NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and further testing identifies serovar L2b.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 7 days
Azithromycin 1 g PO as a single stat dose
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat plus doxycycline for 7 days
Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 21 days
Metronidazole 400 mg PO q12h for 14 days
mcq.e: L1–L3 serovars cause lymphogranuloma venereum, which invades beyond the mucosa; in MSM it mainly presents as haemorrhagic proctitis that can mimic Crohn's disease, often without nodes. Treatment is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days (alternatives: azithromycin 1 g weekly for 3 weeks, or erythromycin for 21 days). Partners from the past 60 days are evaluated, and asymptomatic ones receive doxycycline for 7 days.
w: Wrong - Seven days treats ordinary chlamydia (serovars D–K) but is too short for LGV.
Wrong - A single azithromycin dose is inadequate for invasive LGV.
Wrong - Gonorrhoea cover plus a 7-day course does not adequately treat LGV proctitis.
Correct - LGV is treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days.
Wrong - Metronidazole has no activity against Chlamydia trachomatis.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man has a slowly enlarging ulcer on the prepuce for 3 months. It is painless, beefy red and fleshy, and bleeds easily when touched. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. RPR, TPPA and HSV PCR are negative.
Which investigation will confirm the most likely diagnosis?
o: Gram stain of ulcer scrapings for school-of-fish coccobacilli
Dark-field microscopy of serous exudate from the ulcer
Tissue biopsy with Giemsa or Wright stain for intracellular bodies
Tzanck smear from the ulcer base for multinucleated giant cells
Chlamydia NAAT on the ulcer swab with L-serovar genotyping
mcq.e: A painless, slowly progressive, beefy-red ulcer that bleeds on contact without true lymphadenopathy is typical of donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. It is confirmed by tissue biopsy showing Donovan bodies on Giemsa or Wright stain, or by molecular detection. Treatment is azithromycin 1 g weekly or 500 mg daily for at least 3 weeks or until healed, with follow-up for relapse.
w: Wrong - School-of-fish coccobacilli on Gram stain indicate chancroid, which causes painful ulcers.
Wrong - Dark-field microscopy looks for treponemes; syphilis serology is already negative.
Correct - Biopsy showing Donovan bodies on Giemsa or Wright stain confirms donovanosis.
Wrong - The Tzanck smear relates to herpes, is unreliable, and herpes PCR is negative.
Wrong - LGV causes a transient small ulcer with buboes or proctitis, not a chronic beefy ulcer.
